title: Tristia
text:
1. Little book, you will go to the city without me—and I do not begrudge it—
but, alas for me, your master is not allowed to go!
Go, but unadorned, as befits the book of an exile;
wear, poor thing, the dress that suits this season of mine.
Let no berry-dye veil you in purple stain—
that color does not become a time of mourning—
let no vermilion mark your title, no cedar-oil your page,
nor carry white bosses upon a black brow.
Let such trappings adorn books that are fortunate;
it becomes you to keep my own fortune in mind.
Let no brittle pumice polish your two edges,
that you may go forth shaggy with disordered hair.
Be not ashamed of blots; whoever sees them
will sense that they were made by tears of mine.
Go, book, and greet in my words the places I love:
I will touch them at least with the foot that is allowed me.
If there is anyone among the crowd not forgetful of me,
if anyone who chances to ask how I fare,
you will say that I live, yet deny that I am safe;
and that even my living is a gift I owe to a god.
And so be silent—he who seeks more must read on—
take care lest by chance you speak what is best unspoken!
At once the reader, reminded, will recall my charges,
and I shall be condemned, the public defendant on every tongue.
You take care not to defend me, though words may sting you;
my cause being bad, a pleading would make it worse.
You will find someone who sighs for me, banished,
and reads these poems through with cheeks not dry,
and who, in silence, lest some ill-wisher hear, will wish
that, with Caesar appeased, my punishment grow light.
I too pray that whoever it be may know no misery,
who wishes the gods to be merciful to the wretched;
may what he wishes come to pass, may the prince's anger be lifted,
and may he grant me the power to die in my native land.
Though you carry out my charges, book, you may be blamed,
and be judged below the measure of my talent's praise.
It is the judge's duty to weigh the matter and the time of the matter alike;
the time being weighed, you shall be safe.
Poems come forth drawn out of a serene mind;
my days are clouded with sudden ills,
poems ask for the writer's retirement and leisure;
I am tossed by the sea, the winds, the savage winter.
All fear is hostile to poems; ruined, I look
each moment for the sword to lodge in my throat.
That I do even this, a fair judge will marvel,
and will read what I write, such as it is, with indulgence.
Give me Homer himself and ring him round with so many disasters,
and all his genius would fall away beneath such ills.
In short, remember, book, to go careless of fame,
and feel no shame at having displeased the reader.
Fortune does not so far show herself my friend
that you should keep account of any praise of yours.
While I was unharmed, the love of repute touched me,
and I burned with eagerness to seek a name.
Now let it be enough if I do not hate the poems and the pursuit that harmed me;
thus my exile was won by my own gift.
Yet go you for me, you to whom it is allowed, look upon Rome;
would the gods grant that I might now be my own book!
And do not think, because you come a stranger into the great city,
that you can come unknown to the people.
Though you should lack a title, you are known by your very color;
though you may wish to dissemble, it is plain that you are mine.
Yet enter in secret, lest my poems do you harm;
they are not, as once they were, full of favor.
If there shall be anyone who thinks you, because you are mine,
not worth reading, and casts you from his lap,
say to him, 'Look at the title; I am no teacher of love;
that work has already paid the penalty it earned.'
Perhaps you wonder whether I shall bid you, sent on high,
climb to the Palatine and the house of Caesar.
May the august places and the gods of the place forgive me!
It was from that citadel that the lightning fell upon my head.
I remember indeed that there are most gentle powers
in those abodes, yet I dread the gods who harmed me.
The dove is terrified by the least whir of a wing,
once wounded, hawk, by your talons.
Nor does any lamb dare to wander far from the fold,
once it has been snatched from the teeth of the greedy wolf.
Phaethon, were he alive, would shun the sky, and the horses
he foolishly longed for he would not wish to touch.
I too confess I fear the weapons of Jove I have felt:
I think myself the mark of the hostile fire when it thunders.
Whoever of the Argive fleet escaped Caphereus
ever steered his sails away from the Euboean waters;
and my own bark, once struck by a vast storm,
shudders to approach the place where it was harmed.
Therefore beware, book, and look about with timid mind,
that it may be enough for you to be read by the common folk.
While Icarus sought too lofty heights on feeble wings,
he gave his name to the waters of the sea.
Yet it is hard to say from here whether you should use oars or sail:
the plan, the circumstance, and the place will decide.
If you can be delivered when he is at leisure, if you see all things
mild, if his anger has broken its own force,
if there is anyone who, when you hesitate and fear to approach,
will deliver you, and first speak a few words, then go in.
On a good day, and more fortunate than your master himself,
may you arrive there and lighten my woes.
For these either no one can take away, or only he
who made my wounds, after Achilles' fashion, alone.
Only take care, while you wish to help, that you do no harm—
for my hope is less than my mind's fear—
and beware lest the anger that was at rest, being stirred, blaze again,
and you become a second cause of my punishment!
Yet when you have been taken into my inner room,
and reached your home, the curved bookcase,
you will see your brothers there set out in order,
whom the same toil kept watch and wrought.
The rest of the throng will display their titles openly,
and bear their names upon an uncovered brow;
three you will see far off, hiding in a dark corner—
even so, what no one fails to know, they teach men to love.
These either shun, or, if you have face enough,
contrive to call them by the names of Oedipus and Telegonus.
And of those three, I warn you, if you have any care for your parent,
love none of them, though it should teach you itself.
There are also the changed forms, fifteen rolls,
poems lately snatched from my funeral.
Bid these to say that the look of my own fortune
can be reckoned among the transformed bodies.
For that look has suddenly been made unlike its former self,
now to be wept over, though once it was glad.
More charges, if you ask, I had to give you,
but I fear to have been the cause of slow delay;
and if you were to carry with you, book, all that comes to mind,
you would prove a heavy burden for the bearer.
Long is the way, make haste! For me there is to be dwelt
the world's last edge, a land far removed from my own land.

title: Tristia
text:
2. Gods of sea and sky—for what but prayers is left?—
spare to break apart the timbers of my shattered ship,
and do not, I beg, subscribe to great Caesar's anger!
Often, when one god presses, another god brings aid.
Mulciber was against Troy, for Troy stood Apollo;
Venus was fair to the Trojans, Pallas hostile.
Saturnian Juno, nearer to Turnus, hated Aeneas;
yet he was kept safe by the power of Venus.
Often fierce Neptune assailed wary Ulysses;
often Minerva snatched him from her uncle.
And for me too, though I am far below those men,
what forbids some power to stand by when a god is wroth?
A wretch, I waste idle words that profit nothing.
The heavy waters spatter my very face as I speak,
and the dreadful South Wind hurls away my words, and lets
my prayers not reach the gods to whom they are sent.
So the same winds, lest I be harmed in one way only,
carry off my sails and my vows I know not where.
Wretched me, how great the mountains of water that roll!
Now, now you would think they would touch the highest stars.
How deep the valleys that sink when the sea is parted!
Now, now you would think they would touch black Tartarus.
Wherever I look, there is nothing but sea and sky,
the one swollen with waves, the other threatening with clouds.
Between the two the winds roar with monstrous murmur.
The wave of the sea knows not what master to obey.
For now the East Wind takes its strength from the crimson dawn,
now the West Wind comes, dispatched in the late evening,
now icy Boreas rages from the dry North,
now the South Wind wages his battles full in front.
The helmsman is in doubt, and finds not what to flee or seek:
his very skill is dumbstruck amid the baffling perils.
Surely we perish, and there is no hope of safety,
and as I speak, the wave overwhelms my face.
The flood will crush this life, and with mouth praying in vain
I shall take in the waters that will be my death.
Yet my faithful wife grieves for nothing but my exile:
this one of my ills she knows and bemoans.
She knows not that I am tossed upon the boundless deep,
knows not that I am driven by winds, knows not that death is near.
O it is well that I did not suffer her to embark with me,
lest in my misery I should have to bear death twice!
But now, even if I perish, since she is free of peril,
in half of me at least I shall survive.
Alas, how swift the flame that flashed amid the clouds!
How great the crash that thunders from the height of heaven!
The planks of the sides are struck by the waves no more lightly
than a wall is struck by the heavy weight of a ballista.
This wave that comes rises above all the others:
it is after the ninth and before the eleventh.
I do not fear death; it is the manner of death that is wretched.
Take away the shipwreck, and death will be a gift to me.
It is something, when one falls by his own fate or by the sword,
to lay his dying body upon the solid ground,
to give some charge to his kin and hope for a tomb,
and not to be food for the fishes of the sea.
Suppose me worthy of such a death—I am not alone
borne here. Why does my punishment drag the undeserving down?
O gods above, and you green gods who care for the waters,
let both your throngs now cease your threats,
and the life that Caesar's most gentle anger granted me,
let me carry, unhappy, to the place commanded.
If you wish to destroy me with the punishment I have earned,
my fault, by my own judge, is less than death.
Had Caesar wished already to send me into the Stygian waters,
he had no need of your aid for this.
He has of my blood a store not to be envied;
and what he gave, when he wishes, he himself will take.
But you, whom surely I have harmed by no crime, I think,
be content now, I pray, with my woes!
And yet, though you all should wish to save the wretch,
what has perished can no longer be a head that is safe.
Though the sea grow calm and I have favoring winds,
though you spare me, I shall be no less an exile.
I do not, greedy for endless gain,
plow the wide sea to exchange merchandise,
nor do I seek Athens, which once I sought as a scholar,
nor the towns of Asia, nor places seen before,
nor, carried to Alexander's famous city,
to see your delights, sportive Nile.
That I pray for fair winds—who could believe it?—
it is the Sarmatian land that my sails seek.
I am bound to touch the wild shores of the leftward Pontus;
and I complain that my flight from my country is so slow.
That I may see the Tomitans set in I know not what corner of the world,
I make by my prayers a quick way to a place I shun.
Whether you love me, restrain these mighty floods,
and let your powers be favorable to my ship;
or whether you hate me, drive me on to the appointed land:
part of my punishment lies in the region I seek.
Bear me—what do I here?—swift winds, bear my body away!
Why do my sails long for the Ausonian shores?
Caesar did not wish it; why do you hold him whom he drives forth?
Let the land of Pontus look upon my face.
He bids it, and I have deserved it; nor do I think it right or pious
to defend the charges he has condemned.
Yet if mortal deeds never deceive the gods,
you know that crime is absent from my fault.
Indeed, if you know it so, if my error carried me away,
and my mind was foolish, not wicked,
if—what even the humblest may do—I favored that house,
if Augustus' public commands were enough for me,
if under this leader I spoke of happy ages, and offered
incense for Caesar and the loyal line of Caesars—
if this was my spirit, then spare me, you gods!
If not, let a wave from on high fall and overwhelm my head!
Am I deceived, or do the heavy clouds begin to fade,
and is the wave of the changed sea broken and subdued?
Not by chance, but called under a condition, you gods,
whom none can deceive, you bring me this aid.

title: Tristia
text:
3. When there comes to mind the most sorrowful image of that night,
which was my last hour in the city,
when I recall the night on which I left so many things dear to me,
even now a tear slips from my eyes.
Now the day was near at hand on which Caesar had bidden me
depart from the bounds of farthest Ausonia,
and neither time nor mind had been fit enough for preparing:
my heart had grown numb with the long delay.
I took no thought of choosing slaves or companions,
of fitting clothing or supplies for a fugitive.
I was as stunned as one struck by the fires of Jove,
who lives yet, and is himself unaware of his life.
But when grief itself dispelled this cloud from my mind,
and at last my senses gathered strength,
about to go, I addressed my sorrowing friends one last time,
who, of many, were now but one or two.
My loving wife, weeping, held me, who wept more bitterly still,
with the rain falling ceaselessly down her undeserving cheeks.
My daughter, far away, was apart beneath the Libyan shores,
and could not be told of my fate.
Wherever you looked, grief and groaning sounded,
and within was the look of a funeral that did not keep silence.
Women and men, even children, mourned at my undoing,
and every corner in the house had its tears.
If in small things one may use great examples,
this was the face of Troy in the hour of its capture.
And now the voices of men and dogs were stilled,
and the Moon on high was driving her nocturnal steeds.
Gazing up at her, and beholding by her light the Capitol,
which neighbored my household gods in vain,
I said, 'You powers that dwell in the nearby abodes,
and you temples never again to be seen by my eyes,
and you gods I must leave, whom the lofty city of Quirinus holds,
receive my farewell for all time.
And though I take up the shield late, after my wounds,
yet unburden this exile of your hatred,
and tell the heavenly man what error deceived me,
that he may not think a crime to be a fault,
that the author of my punishment may feel what you know.
With the god appeased, I can cease to be wretched.'
With this prayer I worshipped the gods above; my wife with many more,
her sobs breaking off the words half-spoken.
She too, before the household gods, with hair unbound,
prostrate, touched the dead hearth with trembling lips,
and poured out many words to the adverse Penates,
words of no avail for her lamented husband.
And now the headlong night denied space for delay,
and the Parrhasian Bear had wheeled down from her axis.
What was I to do? I was held back by the sweet love of my country,
but that was the last night before my commanded flight.
Ah, how often, when someone hastened me, I said, 'Why press me?
See either where you hasten to go, or whence.'
Ah, how often I lied that I had a fixed hour
that was fit for the journey I had set.
Three times I touched the threshold, three times I was called back,
and my foot itself, indulging my heart, was slow.
Often, having said farewell, I again spoke many things,
and, as if departing, gave the last of my kisses.
Often I gave the same charges and deceived myself,
looking back with my eyes at the dear pledges of my love.
At last I said, 'Why do I hasten? It is Scythia to which I am sent,
it is Rome that must be left. Each is a just cause for delay.
My wife, alive, is denied to me, alive forever,
and my house, and the sweet members of my faithful house,
and the comrades I have loved with a brother's love,
O hearts joined to me with the faith of Theseus!
While I may, I will embrace you: never, perhaps, will it be allowed
more; the hour granted me is so much gain.'
Without delay, I leave the words of my speech unfinished,
embracing in my heart each one dearest to me.
While I speak and we weep, in the high heaven most brightly,
a star heavy with woe for me, the Morning Star had risen.
I am torn apart no otherwise than if I left my limbs behind,
and a part seemed wrenched away from its own body.
So Mettus grieved when the horses, turned in opposite ways,
were the avengers of his treachery.
Then indeed arose the clamor and the groaning of my people,
and sorrowing hands struck their naked breasts.
Then indeed my wife, clinging to my shoulders as I went,
mingled these sad words with my tears:
'You cannot be torn away. Together, together we shall go,' she said,
'I will follow you, and an exile's wife, an exile I shall be.
For me too the way is made, me too the farthest land receives:
I shall come as a small burden to your fugitive ship.
Caesar's anger bids you depart from your country,
my love bids me; this love shall be my Caesar.'
Such things she attempted, as she had attempted before,
and scarcely yielded her conquered hands to expediency.
I went forth—or rather, that was to be carried out for burial—
squalid, with unkempt hair over my rough face.
She, frenzied with grief, fell, they tell me, as darkness rose before her,
half-lifeless, in the midst of the house.
And when she rose, her hair fouled with vile dust,
and lifted her limbs from the cold ground,
she wept now for herself, now for the deserted Penates,
and often called the name of her husband torn away,
and groaned no less than if she had seen the built-up pyres
holding the body of her daughter or of me;
and she wished to die, to lay down her senses by dying,
yet did not perish, out of regard for me.
Let her live, and, since the fates have so willed, let her live to support
her absent husband ever with her aid.

title: Tristia
text:
4. The Guardian of the Bear of Erymanthus dips into the ocean,
and with his star troubles the waters of the sea.
Yet we cleave the Ionian sea not of our own will,
but are forced by fear to be bold.
Wretched me! With what mighty winds the waters swell,
and the sand, churned from the lowest depths, boils up!
No lower than a mountain, the wave leaps upon the prow
and the curved stern, and lashes the painted gods.
The pine-built planks resound, the rigging shrieks when struck,
and the keel itself groans at my woes.
The sailor, his cold fear confessed by his pallor,
now follows his ship, defeated, no longer guiding it by skill,
and as a feeble rider lets fall the unavailing reins
upon the stiff neck of his horse,
so I see the charioteer give the sails to the ship
not where he wished, but where the rush of the wave drives.
And unless Aeolus send out changed winds,
I shall be borne to places I must now not approach.
For far off, with Illyria left on the left,
forbidden Italy is seen by me.
Let the wind cease, I pray, to strive toward the forbidden lands,
and obey with me the great god.
While I speak, and at once fear and long to be driven back,
with what force the wave struck the side!
Spare me, you blue powers of the sea, spare me,
and let it be enough that Jove is my enemy.
Snatch my weary soul from cruel death,
if only one who has perished can not have perished.
5. O you to be named after no comrades ever,
and to whom my lot seemed your own above all,
who, when I was thunderstruck, were the first, I remember, dearest one,
who dared to sustain me with your words,
who gave me gentle counsel to live,
when in my wretched breast there was a love of death,
you know well to whom I speak, by the tokens set in place of your name,
and your duty, friend, does not escape you.
These things will always be fixed in my deepest marrow,
and I shall be the perpetual debtor of this life,
and my breath shall sooner go to be thinned into the empty air,
and shall leave my bones on the warm pyre,
than forgetfulness of your services steal upon my mind,
and that loyalty of yours fade with the long day.
May the gods be kind to you; may they grant you a fortune
that wants no man's help, and is unlike my own.
Yet if this ship were borne by a friendly wind,
that loyalty of yours would perhaps go unknown.
Pirithous would not have felt Theseus so true a friend
had he not gone living to the infernal waters.
That you should be an example of true love, sad Orestes,
your madness, Phocian, brought it to pass.
Had Euryalus not fallen among the Rutulian foes,
no glory would there be for Nisus, son of Hyrtacus.
Just as tawny gold is tested in the fire,
so in a hard time loyalty must be tried.
While Fortune helps and smiles with serene face,
all things follow undiminished wealth:
but as soon as she thunders, they flee, nor is he known to any
who was lately ringed with troops of companions.
And these things, once gathered from the examples of men of old,
are now known to me as true by my own ills.
Of so many, scarce two or three of you, my friends, are left:
the rest were Fortune's throng, not mine.
The more, O you few, succor my stricken state,
and give safe shores to my shipwreck,
and do not, fearful ones, tremble with false dread
lest the god take offense at this loyalty!
Often Caesar has praised loyalty even in hostile arms,
and loves it in his own, approves it in the foe,
My cause is the better, who fostered no opposing arms,
but earned this flight by my simplicity.
Watch then over my fortunes, I beg,
if any of the god's anger can be diminished.
If anyone desires to know all my misfortunes,
he seeks more than the matter allows to be done.
I have suffered as many ills as there are stars shining in the sky,
and as many bodies as the dry dust holds;
and I have borne much that is greater than belief, and that,
though it has befallen, will not be believed.
Even a part of it must die with me,
and I would that it could be hidden while I conceal it.
If I had an unbreakable voice, a breast firmer than bronze,
and many mouths with many tongues,
not even so could I embrace all in words,
the matter surpassing my strength.
Write of my woes, learned poets, in place of the Neritian chief:
for I have borne more woes than the Neritian.
He in a short span wandered through many years
between the homes of Dulichium and of Ilium:
me, having measured seas distant by all the stars,
fate has borne to the Getic and Sarmatian gulfs.
He had a faithful band and loyal comrades:
me, a fugitive, my companions deserted.
He, glad and victorious, sought his native land:
I, conquered and an exile, fled from my country.
And I have no home in Dulichium or Ithaca or Samos,
places from which to be absent is no great punishment,
but the one which from its seven hills surveys the whole world,
Rome, the seat of empire and of the gods.
He had a body hard and patient of toils:
my strength is feeble and gently bred.
He was ceaselessly driven amid savage arms:
I myself was accustomed to gentle pursuits.
A god has crushed me, with none to lighten my woes:
a warrior goddess brought him aid.
And though he who reigns in the swelling waters is less than Jove,
him Neptune's anger pressed, me the anger of Jove.
Add that the greatest part of his toils is fiction;
in my woes there is no fable.
At last he reached the home he had sought,
and gained, after all, the fields he had long sought:
but I must forever be deprived of my native earth,
unless the anger of the wronged god grow softer.

title: Tristia
text:
6. Not so dearly was Lyde loved by the Clarian poet,
nor so dearly Bittis loved by her Coan,
as you, my wife, cling to my breast,
worthy of a less wretched husband, not a better one.
Upon you my ruin has rested, as on a beam set beneath it:
if I am still anything, all is your gift.
You make it that I am not despoiled, nor stripped by those
who sought the planks of my shipwreck.
And as a ravening wolf, goaded by hunger and greedy for blood,
seizes upon a sheepfold left unguarded,
or as the devouring vulture looks about for some body
that it may spy laid out beneath no earth,
so someone, false to me in my bitter circumstances,
would have come upon my goods, had you allowed it.
Your courage, through brave friends, drove him off,
to whom no worthy thanks can be returned.
Therefore he proves it, by a witness as wretched as true,
if only such a witness has any weight.
Neither Hector's wife is before you in uprightness,
nor Laodamia, companion of her husband in death.
Had you been allotted the Maeonian bard,
the fame of Penelope would be second to yours:
whether you owe this to yourself, made loyal with no teacher,
and your character was given you with the new light,
or whether the woman who is first, honored by you through all the years,
teaches you to be the example of a good wife,
and has made you like herself by long acquaintance,
if it is allowed to liken small things to great—
alas for me, that my poems have no great strength,
and that my words are too small for your deserts!—
and that, if there was once any living vigor in me,
it is all quenched, fallen beneath my long woes!—
otherwise you would hold first place among the holy heroines,
first would you be seen for the goodness of your soul.
Yet, however far my praises shall avail,
you shall live in my poems for all time.
7. Whoever you are who have features like mine in a portrait,
take the ivy, Bacchus' garlands, from my hair.
Those fortunate emblems become happy poets:
a crown is not fit for times like mine.
Conceal this from yourself, yet feel it spoken, best of men,
you who turn and return me upon your finger,
and, clasping my likeness in tawny gold,
look upon the dear face, such as you may, of the banished.
As often as you gaze on it, the thought may come to you to say,
'How far from us is Naso, my comrade!'
Your devotion is welcome, but my poems are the greater image
of me, which I bid you read, such as they are,
poems that tell of the changed shapes of men,
a work that the master's unhappy flight broke off.
These, as I departed, like many of my things,
I myself, in sorrow, laid with my own hand upon the fire.
And as the Thestian, they tell, burned her son in the brand,
and was a better sister than a mother,
so I laid the undeserving little books, doomed to perish with me,
my own flesh, upon the swift pyre:
whether because I hated the Muses, as my own crimes,
or because the poem was still growing and unfinished.
And since these were not utterly destroyed, but survive—
I think they were written out in many copies—
now I pray that they may live, and that they may delight
the reader's not idle leisure, and remind him of me.
Yet they will not be read with patience by anyone
who does not know that the final hand is missing from them.
That work was taken from the midst of the anvils,
and the last file was wanting to my writings.
And I ask pardon in place of praise: I am praised enough
if I am not scorned by you, reader.
These six verses too, if you think they should be set
at the very front of the little book, take them.
"Whoever you are who touch these rolls bereft of their parent,
to these at least let a place be given in your city.
And that you may favor them the more, these were not published by him,
but snatched, as it were, from their master's funeral.
Whatever fault, therefore, this rough poem shall have,
I would have amended, had it been allowed."

title: Tristia
text:
8. Into their own springs shall the deep rivers glide back from the sea,
and the Sun, with horses reversed, shall run backward:
the earth shall bear stars, the sky be cleft by the plow,
the wave shall give flames, and fire give water,
all things shall go contrary to the laws of nature,
and no part of the world shall keep its own course,
all things shall now happen which I denied could happen,
and there is nothing in which faith should not be placed.
This I prophesy, because I am deceived by him
whom I thought would bring aid to me, wretched.
Did so great a forgetfulness of me seize you, false one,
and was it so great a fear to approach me, afflicted,
that you neither looked back nor consoled me, fallen,
hard man, nor followed my funeral train?
Does that holy and venerable name of friendship
lie for you a thing of no worth, beneath your feet?
What was it to visit a comrade laid low by a vast weight,
and lighten him in part with your words,
and, if not to let fall a tear over my misfortunes,
yet to bear a few words of feigned grief,
and at least to say—what even strangers do—
and follow the voice of the people and the public talk—
finally, to behold my mournful face, never to be seen again,
while you might on that last day,
and to hear, once and never more in all your life,
the word that had to be said, and return it with an equal "farewell"?
But others did, joined to me by no bond,
and gave the tears that are the tokens of their hearts.
What, if I had not been joined to you by companionship and strong ties
and the love of a long time?
What, if you had not known so many of my jests and so many of my cares,
and I myself had not known so many of your jests and cares?
What, if you had been known to me only at Rome,
admitted so often into every kind of place?
Have all these things gone vain into the sea-winds?
Are all sunk and borne off in the waters of Lethe?
I do not think you were born in the peaceful city of Quirinus,
the city my foot may now no longer approach,
but among the crags which the leftward Pontus holds here,
and on the wild ridges of Scythia and Sarmatia:
veins of flint are round your heart,
and your hard breast holds the seeds of iron,
and the nurse who once gave you, to draw with tender palate,
her full breasts, was a tigress:
or you would think my woes less alien than now you do,
and I would not arraign you as guilty of hardness.
But since this too is added to my fated losses,
that my first days lack their proper measures,
make me not remember this offense, and let me praise
your service with the very lips with which I now complain.
9. May it be granted you to reach the goal of life unhindered,
you who read this work of mine without enmity.
And would that my prayers could avail for you,
which for me did not touch the hard gods!
While you are unharmed, you will count many friends:
if the times grow cloudy, you will be alone.
You see how the doves come to white roofs,
how the dingy tower receives no birds.
The ants never make for empty granaries:
no friend will come to wealth that is lost.
And as the shadow accompanies those who walk in the sun's rays,
but flees when he hides, pressed by clouds,
so the fickle crowd follows the lights of Fortune:
when these are covered, night drawn over them, it departs.
I pray that these things may always seem false to you;
yet by my own case they must be confessed true.
While I stood, my house, known indeed but not ambitious,
had crowd enough,
but as soon as it was struck, all feared its ruin,
and warily turned their backs in common flight.
I do not wonder that they fear the savage thunderbolts,
by whose fires whatever is nearest is wont to be scorched,
yet Caesar approves a friend who remains in hard times,
however hateful the foe,
nor is he wont to be angry—for none is more moderate—
when one, in adversity, still loves what he loved.
When Thoas had learned of the comrade of Argive Orestes,
he himself, they tell, approved of Pylades.
The loyalty that was ever between the son of Actor and great Achilles
was wont to be praised by the lips of Hector.
That loyal Theseus went as a comrade to the shades with his friend,
they say the god of Tartarus grieved.
When the loyalty of Euryalus and Nisus was told to you, Turnus,
it is credible that your cheeks were wet with tears.
There is loyalty even in the wretched, and it is approved in a foe—
alas for me, how few these words of mine move!
Such is my state, such now is the fortune of my affairs,
that there should be no measure to my tears,
yet my breast, though most saddened by its own fall,
has been made serene by your advancement.
This I saw would come, dearest one, even then,
when a fairer wind still bore your ship along,
whether there is some price in character or in a life
free from stain, no one was to be bought for more:
or whether one has lifted his head through the noble arts—
any cause is made good by your eloquence.
Stirred by these things, I said to you at once yourself,
"A great stage awaits your gifts, my friend."
This was told me not by the entrails of sheep or the thunder on the left,
nor by the cry or wing of a watched bird:
reason is my augury, and conjecture of the future:
by this I divined and gained my knowledge.
And since it is true, with all my heart I congratulate
you and myself that your talent did not lie hidden.
But would that mine had lain hidden in deepest darkness!
It had profited my pursuit that the light were absent.
And as the stern arts profit you, eloquent one,
so unlike arts have harmed me.
Yet my life is known to you. You know that from those arts
their author kept his own conduct apart.
You know this poem was an old sport of my youth, and that those
jests, though not to be praised, were yet but jests.
Therefore, as I think my crimes can be defended by no color,
so I think they can be excused.
Excuse them as you can, and do not forsake your friend's cause:
as you have well begun, so may you ever go on well.

title: Tristia
text:
10. I have, and may I keep, I pray, the guardianship of yellow-haired Minerva,
and my ship has its name from the painted helmet.
Whether there is need of sails, she runs well to the lightest breeze,
or whether of the oar, she makes her way by the rower.
Not content to outrun her fellows in winged course,
she overtakes the ships that have set out however far before,
and bears alike the waves and the seas leaping far,
nor, conquered, does she grow waterlogged by the savage waters.
She, first known to me at Cenchreae of Corinth,
remains faithful, leader and companion of my fearful flight,
and through so many chances and seas stirred by hostile winds,
was kept safe by the power of Pallas.
Now too, I pray, may she safely cut the mouths of the vast Pontus,
and enter the waters of the Getic shore that she seeks.
When she had brought me down to the sea of Aeolian Helle,
and made the long journey by a narrow track,
we bent our course to the left, and from the city of Hector
we came to your harbors, land of Imbros.
Thence, with a light wind reaching the Zerynthian shores,
the weary keel touched Thracian Samos.
From here it is a short leap to Tempyra for one bound across:
thus far did she follow her master.
For it pleased me to traverse the Bistonian plains on foot:
she retraced the Hellespontine waters
and made for Dardania, which bears its founder's name,
and you, Lampsacus, kept safe by the rustic god,
and the strait which, where the maiden was ill carried across the narrow waves,
separates Sestos from the Abydene city,
and Cyzicus, clinging to the Propontine shores,
Cyzicus, the noble work of the Haemonian race,
and the Byzantine shores that hold the jaws of Pontus:
this is the vast gateway of the twin sea.
These, I pray, may she overcome, and, driven by strong south winds,
may she briskly pass the shifting Cyanean rocks
and the Thynian gulfs, and from these by Apollo's city
direct her course beneath the close walls of Anchialus.
Thence may she pass the Mesembrian harbors and Odessus and the citadels
named with your name, Bacchus,
and those whom they say, sprung from the walls of Alcathous,
set up their household gods as fugitives in these abodes,
from whom may she come safe to the Milesian city,
where the wrath of an offended god has carried me.
If these things befall, a lamb shall fall for deserving Minerva:
a greater victim does not suit my means.
You too, sons of Tyndareus, brothers whom this island honors,
I pray, be present, gentle powers, to the twofold way!
For one of our ships prepares to go through the narrow Symplegades,
the other to cleave the Bistonian waters.
Grant that, when we seek diverse places,
the one may have her winds, and no less the other hers.
11. Every letter you have read in this whole little book
was made by me in the anxious time of my journey.
Either the Adriatic saw me writing these, amid its waters,
while I shivered in the cold month of December,
or, after I had crossed by my course the twin-sea Isthmus,
and a second keel was taken for my flight,
that I made verses amid the wild murmurs of the sea,
I think the Aegean Cyclades stood amazed.
I myself now marvel that, amid such tumults of mind and sea,
my talent did not fail.
Whether numbness or madness is the name for this pursuit,
by this care all my care is lightened.
Often I was tossed in doubt by the stormy Kids,
often the sea was threatening with the star of Sterope,
and the Guardian of the Atlantean Bear darkened the day,
or the South Wind had drained the Hyades of their late rains,
often the sea was within the ship, yet I myself
drew out my poems, such as they are, with trembling hand.
Now too the rigging shrieks, taut with the North Wind,
and the hollowed water rises in the shape of a mound.
The helmsman himself, lifting his palms to the stars,
forgetful of his skill, demands aid with prayers.
Wherever I look, there is nothing but the image of death,
which with doubtful mind I fear, and fearing, pray for.
Should I reach harbor, I shall be terrified by the harbor itself:
the hostile land holds more of fear than the water.
For I labor at once under the snares of men and of the sea,
and the sword and the wave make my twin terrors.
The one I dread will hope for plunder from my blood,
the other will wish to have the glory of my death.
The leftward part is barbarous, and used to greedy plunder,
which gore and slaughter and wars ever hold,
and though the sea is stirred by the wintry waves,
their breasts are more troubled than the sea itself.
So much the more should you forgive these poems, candid reader,
if they are, as they are, below your hope.
These I did not write, as once, in my gardens,
nor, accustomed couch, do you hold my body.
I am tossed in the untamed deep on a winter's day,
and the very page is struck by the dark-blue waters.
The cruel storm fights and is indignant that I dare
to write while it shakes its rigid threats.
Let the storm conquer the man! But at the same time, I beg,
let me set an end to my song, and it to its own.

title: Tristia
text:
1. What have I to do with you, unhappy concern, my little books,
I who, wretched, have perished by my own talent?
Why do I return to the now-condemned Muses, my own offense?
Is it too little to have once deserved punishment?
Poems made man and woman wish to know me,
by no fortunate omen of mine;
poems made Caesar mark me and my conduct,
bidding my Art be already taken from me.
Take from me my pursuit, and you take the offenses of my life too;
I lay it to the verses that I am guilty.
This is the reward I won for my care and my wakeful toils:
punishment was found for my talent.
Had I been wise, I should rightly have hated the learned sisters,
powers ruinous to their own worshipper.
But now—so great a madness is the companion of my disease—
I bring my luckless foot back again to those rocks:
just as the conquered gladiator seeks the arena again,
and the shipwrecked vessel returns to the swelling waters.
Perhaps, as once for him who held the realm of Teuthras,
so the same thing shall bring me both wound and cure,
and the Muse, who roused the anger, shall also soothe it when roused;
poems often entreat the great gods.
Caesar himself bade the Ausonian mothers and brides
sing poems to turret-crowned Ops.
He had bidden them sung to Phoebus too, at the time when he held the games
which one age looks upon but once.
By these examples I pray that now, most gentle Caesar,
your anger may be made milder by my talent.
That anger is just, and I will not deny I deserved it—
shame has not so far fled from my face—
but unless I had sinned, what could you pardon?
My lot gave you the matter for mercy.
If, as often as men sin, Jupiter should hurl his thunderbolts,
in a short time he would be unarmed;
now, when he has thundered and terrified the world with his crash,
he gives back the air pure, the rains scattered.
Rightly therefore is he called father and ruler of the gods,
rightly the spacious world has nothing greater than Jove.
You too, since you are called ruler and father of your country,
use the way of the god who bears the same name.
And this you do; nor could any man ever
hold the reins of his empire more temperately.
You have often granted pardon to the conquered side,
which he, the victor, would not have granted to you.
I have seen many enriched with wealth and honors
who had borne arms against your head;
and the day that ended the war ended your anger for the war,
and both sides at once brought gifts to the temples;
and as your soldier rejoices that he has conquered the foe,
so the foe has cause to rejoice that he was conquered.
My cause is the better, who am not said to have followed
opposing arms nor a hostile cause.
By the sea, by the lands, by the third powers I swear,
by you, a god present and beheld,
that this heart favored you, greatest of men, and that I,
so far as I alone could, was yours in mind.
I prayed that you might reach the heavenly stars but late,
and I was a small part of the throng that prayed the same,
and I offered pious incense for you, and with all the rest, alone,
I too aided the public prayers with my own.
Why should I tell that my books—those too, my offense—
are full of your name in a thousand places?
Look at the greater work, which is still held unfinished,
of bodies changed into forms past belief:
you will find there the praises of your name,
you will find there many pledges of my heart.
Your glory is not made greater by poems, nor has it room
to grow that it might be made greater;
Jove's fame more than suffices: yet it pleases him that his deeds
be told, and that he himself be the matter of song,
and when the battles of the war with the Giants are recounted,
it is credible that he is glad at his own praises.
Others celebrate you, as is fitting, with what voice they can,
and sing your praises with richer genius:
yet, just as a god is won by the shed blood of a hundred bulls,
so he is won by the least offering of incense.
Ah, fierce and to me crueler than all my foes,
whoever read out to you my delights,
that the poems honoring you in my books
might not be read with a fairer judgment.
But who could be my friend while you were angry?
Scarcely then was I not an enemy to myself.
When the shaken house has begun to sink, the whole weight
settles upon the leaning parts,
and all things gape when fortune makes a crack,
and, dragged by their own weight, fall to ruin.
So I won the hatred of men by my poem, and the crowd
followed your face, as it had to.
Yet, I remember, you approved my life and conduct,
by the horse you had given me, as I passed in review.
And if this profits nothing, and no glory of honor
is returned, yet I had won no charge of crime.
Nor was the fortune of defendants ill committed to me,
to be examined by the Hundred Men.
Private affairs too I judged without blame,
and even the losing side confessed my good faith.
Wretched me! I could, had not the last things harmed me,
have been safe by your judgment more than once.
The last things ruin me, and beneath the lowest sea
one storm sinks the ship so often unharmed.
Nor did a small part of the flood harm me, but all
the waves and the ocean pressed upon this head.
Why did I see anything? Why did I make my eyes guilty?
Why was the fault known to me, unwitting?
Unknowing, Actaeon saw Diana unclothed:
none the less he was the prey of his own hounds.
Surely among the gods even chance must be atoned for,
nor does mischance find pardon when a power is wronged.
On that day on which an evil error carried me off,
my house, small indeed, but without stain, was ruined:
so too, though small, let it be called illustrious in our fathers' age,
and inferior to none in nobility,
and to be marked neither for wealth nor for poverty,
so that from neither was a knight to be conspicuous.
Though my house be small in fortune or in birth,
yet by my talent it is surely not unknown,
which, though I may seem to have used too youthfully,
yet I bear a great name from all the world,
and the throng of the learned knows Naso, and dares
to number him among men not despised.
This house, then, dear to the Muses, has fallen, brought low
by a single, but no slight, offense:
and it has so fallen that it may rise, if only the anger
of the wronged Caesar shall ripen to its end,
in the issue of whose punishment there is such mercy
that it has come milder than my fear.
Life was granted me, and your anger stopped short of death,
O prince, sparing in the use of your might!
Besides, my father's wealth is added, you not taking it away,
as though life were too small a gift.
You did not condemn my deeds by a decree of the senate,
nor was my flight ordered by a chosen judge.
Inveighing with grim words—as befits a prince—
you yourself avenged your wrongs, as is fitting.
Add that the edict, though harsh and threatening,
was yet mild in the name of the penalty;
for in it I am called relegated, not an exile,
and the words there are proper to my fortune.
No penalty, indeed, is heavier to a sane man and one of sound mind,
than to have displeased so great a man;
but a divine power is wont sometimes to be appeasable:
when the cloud is driven off, the bright day is wont to come.
I have seen an elm laden with leafy vines
which had been struck by the bolt of savage Jove.
Though you yourself forbid me to hope, I will hope on;
this one thing can be done though you forbid it.
A great hope steals upon me when I look on you, most gentle prince,
hope fails me when I look back on my own deeds.
And as, when the winds stir the air, there is no
unbroken fury and continual rage,
but at times they subside and, intermitting, grow still,
and you would think they had laid aside their force:
so my fears go and come and vary,
and grant and deny me the hope of appeasing you.
Therefore by the gods above, who grant and will grant you
long ages, if only they love the Roman name,
by your country, which is safe and secure under you, its parent,
of which, among the people, I was lately a part,
so may the love it owes you, the city's love,
be returned to you, who ever deserve it by your deeds and heart;
so may Livia complete her wedded years with you,
who, but for you, was worthy of no husband,
who, were she not, the single life would become you,
and there was none to whom you could be a husband;
safe with you may your son be safe too, and one day
rule this empire, an old man with you, an older one;
and as your grandsons do, the youthful stars,
may they walk by your deeds and by their father's;
so may Victory, accustomed always to your camp,
now too present herself and seek your familiar standards,
and circle about the Ausonian leader on her wonted wings,
and lay the laurel garland on his shining hair,
through whom you wage your wars, in whose body you now fight,
to whom you give great auspices and your own gods,
and with half of yourself you are present and behold the city,
with half you are far off and wage savage wars;
so may he return to you a victor over the conquered foe,
and shine aloft on the garlanded horses—
spare, I beg, and put away your thunderbolt, your fierce weapons,
weapons, alas, too well known to wretched me!
Spare, father of your country, nor, forgetful of this name,
take from me the hope of one day appeasing you.
I do not pray to return, though it is credible that the great gods
have often granted things greater than was asked;
if you give a milder exile, and nearer, to me who beg it,
a great part of my punishment will be lightened.
I endure the utmost, cast out among hostile foes,
nor is any exile farther from his country than I,
sent alone to the mouths of the sevenfold Hister,
pressed beneath the icy pole of the Parrhasian maiden—
the Cizyges and Colchi and the throng of Teretei and the Getae
are scarcely kept off by the waters between the Danube—
and, though others have been banished for a graver cause,
to none was a farther land given than to me.
Beyond this there is nothing but cold and foes,
and the wave that freezes with binding frost.
Thus far is the Roman part of the leftward Euxine:
the Basternae and Sauromatae hold the next.
This is the last land under Ausonian law, and scarcely
clings to the margin of your empire.
Whence I pray, a suppliant, that you relegate me to safety,
that peace too may not be taken from me with my country,
that I may not fear the tribes which the Hister ill keeps off,
nor that I, your citizen, may be captured by the foe.
Divine law forbids that any born of Latin blood
should suffer barbarian chains while the Caesars are safe.
Though two charges have ruined me, a poem and an error,
the guilt of the one deed must be kept silent.
For I am not of such worth as to renew your wounds, Caesar,
who have grieved once more than too much.
The other part remains, in which, made by a shameful poem,
I am accused of being the teacher of foul adultery.
It is possible, then, for heavenly minds to be deceived in some things,
and there are many beneath your notice;
and as for Jove, gazing at once upon the gods and the lofty sky,
there is no leisure to attend to trifling matters,
so, while you survey the world that hangs upon you,
lesser things escape your cares.
Should the prince of empire, leaving his post,
read poems made in unequal measures?
The weight of the Roman name does not so press upon you,
and so light a burden is borne on your shoulders,
that you can turn your divine power to silly trifles,
and run over my leisure with your eyes.
Now Pannonia, now the Illyrian shore must be tamed,
now Raetian and Thracian arms cause fear,
now the Armenian seeks peace, now the Parthian horseman
holds out his bow and the captured standards with timid hand,
now Germany feels you young again through your offspring,
and a Caesar wages wars for the great Caesar;
in short, as in so great a body—greater than ever was—
there is no part of the empire that wavers.
The city too wearies you, and the guardianship of your laws
and of morals, which you wish to be like your own.
Nor do you enjoy the leisure you grant to the nations,
and you wage unresting wars with many.
Should I wonder, then, that in this weight of so great affairs
you have never unrolled my jests?
But if, as I would prefer, you had chanced to have leisure,
you would have read no crime in my Art.
That writing, I confess, is not of a stern brow,
nor worthy to be read by so great a prince:
yet it is not for that contrary to the commands of the laws,
nor does it instruct Roman brides.
And that you may not doubt for whom I wrote the little books,
one of the three has these four verses:
"Be far off, slender fillets, the emblem of modesty,
and you, long flounce, that cover the middle of the feet!
I shall sing nothing but the lawful and permitted loves,
and in my poem there shall be no crime."
Have I not strictly barred from this Art all
whom the matron's robe and the fillet forbid to be touched?
But the matron can use the arts of others, and has,
though she be not taught, what she may draw from them.
Then let the matron read nothing, for by any poem
she can be made more learned for offending.
Whatever she touches, if she is bent on evil,
from it she will fashion her ways to vice.
Let her take up the Annals—nothing is rougher than they—
and surely she will read how Ilia became a mother;
let her take up "Mother of the line of Aeneas" at the first,
and she will ask whence kindly Venus was mother of the line of Aeneas.
I will pursue it below, if only I am allowed to go in order,
that every kind of writing can harm the mind.
Yet not for that will every book bear a charge:
nothing is profitable that cannot likewise harm.
What is more useful than fire? Yet if one prepares
to burn houses, he arms his bold hands with fire.
Medicine sometimes takes away, sometimes gives, health,
and shows which herb helps and which is harmful.
Both the robber and the wary traveler are girded with a sword;
the one carries snares, the other aid for himself.
Eloquence is learned that it may plead innocent causes;
it protects the guilty, and oppresses the undeserving.
So my poem, if read with an upright mind,
will be found able to harm no one.
"But it corrupts some." Whoever holds this is wrong,
and claims too much for my writings.
Yet, that I may grant this—the games too supply the seeds
of wickedness: bid all the theaters be taken away!
The Martial sand, when it strews the hard ground with blood,
how often it has given many a cause for sin!
Let the Circus be removed! The Circus's license is not safe.
Here a girl sits next to a man unknown.
Since some women walk here, that a lover may meet
in the same place, why does any portico lie open?
What place is more august than the temples? Let her shun these too,
if any woman is ingenious for her own undoing.
When she stands in the shrine of Jove, in the shrine of Jove it will occur to her
how many mothers that god has made.
As she enters the neighboring temple of Juno to adore,
how this goddess grieved over his many rivals.
With Pallas in view, she will ask why the maid took up
Erichthonius, born of a crime.
Let her come into the temple of great Mars, your gift,
and Venus stands joined to the Avenger, her husband before the doors.
Sitting in the shrine of Isis, she will ask why the Saturnian
drove her across the Ionian and Bosphorian sea.
Anchises will be a precedent for Venus, the Latmian hero for the Moon,
Iasion for Ceres, that may be cited.
All things can corrupt perverted minds;
yet all things stand safe in their own places,
and far from immodest women the first page sets up
my Art, written for harlots alone, and bars the hands of the chaste.
Whatever woman bursts where the priest does not allow her to go,
straightway she herself is guilty of the charge she took on.
Yet it is no crime to unroll tender verses;
the chaste may read much that is not to be done.
Often a matron of stern brow looks upon
naked women and Venus standing ready for every kind.
Vestal eyes behold harlots' bodies,
nor was that a cause of punishment to their owner.
But why is there too much wantonness in my Muse,
and why does my book persuade anyone to love?
Nothing but my sin and manifest fault must be confessed:
I repent of my talent and my judgment.
Why did I not rather sing of Troy, fallen
beneath the Argive arms, and harassed again by my poem?
Why was I silent of Thebes and the mutual wounds of brothers,
and the seven gates, each under its own leader?
Nor did warlike Rome deny me matter,
and it is a pious toil to record one's country's deeds.
In short, since you, Caesar, have filled all things with your merits,
one of the many parts should have been sung by me,
and as the radiant lights of the sun draw the eyes,
so your deeds should have drawn my mind.
I am blamed unjustly; a thin field is plowed by me;
that was a work of great fertility.
A little boat should not trust itself to the deep
because it dares to sport on a small lake.
Perhaps—and even this I doubt—I am fit enough
for the lighter measures, and suffice for the small modes:
but if you should bid me tell of the Giants tamed by Jove's fire,
the burden will cripple me as I attempt it.
It is for a rich genius to set down the boundless deeds of Caesar,
lest the work be overwhelmed by its matter.
And yet I had dared; but I seemed to disparage,
and—what is impious—to do harm to your might.
I came back again to the light work, the poems of my youth,
and stirred my heart with a feigned love.
I would not, indeed, but my fates dragged me on,
and I was ingenious for my own punishment.
Alas for me, that I learned! Why did my parents teach me,
and why did any letters detain my eyes?
This wantonness made me hateful to you, for the Art
by which you thought I tempted forbidden beds.
But brides did not learn deceptions with me for master,
and no one can teach what he scarcely knows.
So I made my delights and tender poems
that no tale ever grazed my name.
Nor is there any husband, even of the common folk,
who through my fault is in doubt of his fatherhood.
Believe me, my conduct differs from my poem—
my life is modest, my Muse is playful—
and the greater part of my works is lying and feigned:
it has allowed itself more than its author.
Nor is a book the index of the mind, but an honest pleasure
bringing much that is fit to charm the ear.
Else Accius would be savage, Terence a reveler,
and those who sing wild wars would be quarrelsome.
In short, I am not alone in having composed tender loves:
for love composed, I alone have paid the penalty.
What did the Teian Muse of the lyric old man teach
but to confound Venus with much wine?
What did Lesbian Sappho teach the girls but to love?
Yet Sappho was safe, and he too was safe.
Nor did it harm you, son of Battus, that often, as you read,
you confessed in verse your own delights.
No play of pleasant Menander is without love,
and he is wont to be read to boys and girls.
The Iliad itself, what is it but an adulteress, over whom
there was a battle between her lover and her husband?
What comes first in it but the passion for Briseis, and how
the ravished girl made the leaders wroth?
Or what is the Odyssey but a woman, sought by many suitors
for love while her husband is away?
Who but Homer tells of Venus and Mars bound,
their bodies caught upon a shameful bed?
Whence but by great Homer's testimony should we know
that two goddesses burned for their guest?
Tragedy surpasses every kind of writing in gravity:
this too ever has the matter of love.
For what is there in Hippolytus but the passion of the blind stepmother?
Canace is renowned for the love of her own brother.
What? Did not the Tantalid, with Cupid driving his chariot,
carry off the Pisan maid behind his ivory Phrygian steeds?
That a mother dipped her sword in her children's blood,
grief, roused by wounded love, did it; love made
the king and his rival suddenly into birds,
and the mother who still now mourns her Itys.
Had not the wicked brother loved Aerope,
we should not read of the Sun's averted steeds.
Nor would impious Scylla have touched the tragic buskin,
had not love cut her father's lock.
You who read of Electra and Orestes out of his mind,
read of Aegisthus' crime and the Tyndarid's.
For why should I tell of the grim tamer of the Chimaera,
whom a treacherous hostess nearly gave to death?
Why should I speak of Hermione, of you, maid of Schoeneus,
and of you, prophetess loved by the Mycenaean chief?
Why of Danae and Danae's daughter-in-law and the mother of Lyaeus,
and Haemon, and her for whom two nights were joined?
Why of the son-in-law of Pelias, of Theseus, and of him
who first of the Pelasgians touched the Trojan ground from his ship?
Add to these Iole and the parent of Pyrrhus, add Hercules' wife,
add Hylas and the Trojan boy.
Time will fail me if I pursue the tragic fires,
and my book will scarce hold the bare names.
Tragedy too is mixed with foul laughter,
and has many words of forgotten modesty;
nor did it harm the author who made Achilles soft,
to have broken his brave deeds by his measures.
Aristides joined the Milesian crimes to himself,
yet Aristides was not driven from his city.
Nor did Eubius, author of an impure history,
who described how the seeds of mothers are corrupted, flee;
nor did he who lately composed the Sybaritica,
nor those who did not keep silent of their own embraces.
And these things are mingled with the monuments of learned men,
and by the gifts of leaders the public deeds lie open.
And lest I should defend myself only by foreign arms,
the Roman book too has much that is playful,
and as grave Ennius sang Mars with his own lips—
Ennius greatest in genius, rude in art—
as Lucretius unfolds the causes of swift fire,
and prophesies the threefold work's fall,
so the woman, to whom Lesbia was a false name,
was often sung by wanton Catullus;
nor content with that, he published many loves,
in which he confessed his own adultery.
Equal and like was the license of slender Calvus,
who disclosed his own intrigues in various measures.
Why should I tell of the poems of Ticidas, of Memmius, in whom
there is a name for the things and shame for the names?
Cinna too is their comrade, and Anser bolder than Cinna,
and the light work of Cornificius, and Cato's like.
And in whose books Perilla, lately dissembled
by name, is now read called by yours, Metellus.
He too, who led the Argo into the Phasian waters,
could not keep silent of his own stolen loves of Venus.
No less wanton are the poems of Hortensius, no less
those of Servius—who would doubt to follow names so plain?
Sisenna turned Aristides, nor did it harm him
to have inserted shameful jests into history.
It was no reproach to Gallus to have celebrated Lycoris,
but not to have held his tongue when too full of wine.
Tibullus thinks it hard to believe one who swears,
since likewise she denies to her husband concerning herself.
He confesses he himself taught how to deceive the guards,
and now says, wretched, that he is pressed by his own art.
Often, as if he were proving his mistress's gem or seal,
he remembers, on that pretext, to have touched her hand;
and, as he relates, he often spoke with fingers and a nod,
and traced a silent mark on the round of the table,
and teaches by what juices the bruise leaves the body,
which is wont to be made by the pressing of the mouth:
in short, he asks of the too-careless husband
that he watch his wife too, that she may sin the less,
he knows at whom the dog barks when he walks alone,
why he so often plies the closed doors before her,
and gives many such precepts of intrigue, and teaches
by what art brides can deceive their husbands;
this was no fraud to him, and Tibullus is read
and pleases, and was already known when you were prince.
You will find the same alluring precepts in Propertius:
yet he is grazed by not the least mark.
These I succeeded, since candor bids me hide
the illustrious names of the living,
I did not fear, I confess, that, where so many keels have gone,
mine alone should be wrecked while all the rest are saved.
Arts are written by others by which the dice are played:—
this was no slight crime to our forefathers—
what the knuckle-bones avail, by what throw you may
fix the most, and escape the ruinous "dogs";
what numbers the die has, when, the throw called,
it is fitting to cast, and how to handle the cast;
how the parti-colored piece may advance on the straight line,
when the man between two foes is lost,
how the one following knows to wage war and recall the one before,
nor flee unaccompanied in safety,
how the small board is set with three pebbles a side,
on which to have won is to have kept one's own in a row,
and the other games—for I will not now pursue them all—
that are wont to waste our time, a precious thing.
Lo, another sings, glad, of the shapes of balls,
this one teaches the art of swimming, that one of the hoop.
By others the care of dyeing the complexion is composed,
this one has given laws for banquets and hospitality;
another shows the clay from which cups are shaped,
and teaches what jar is fit for clear wine.
Such things are played in smoky December,
which it was harm to none to have composed.
Deceived by these, I made poems not sad,
but a sad punishment has followed my jests.
In short, of so many writers I do not see one
whom his own Muse has ruined; I am the one found.
What if I had written mimes jesting at obscene things,
which ever have the crime of forbidden love,
in which the well-dressed adulterer steadily comes forth,
and the cunning wife cheats her foolish husband?
The marriageable maid, the matron, the man, the boy
look on, and a great part of the senate is present,
nor is it enough that the ears are profaned by lewd words;
the eyes grow used to suffering many shameful things;
and when the lover has cheated the husband by some novelty,
he is applauded, and the palm given with great favor;
and what profits less, the stage is lucrative for the poet,
and the praetor buys such crimes at no small price.
Look at the cost of your own games, Augustus:
you will read that you have bought many such things at great cost.
These you have watched, and often given to be watched—
so kindly everywhere is your majesty—
and with your eyes, which the whole world uses,
you have looked, unmoved, upon adulteries on the stage.
If it is right to write mimes imitating shameful things,
the punishment due to my matter is less.
Or does this kind of writing make its boards safe,
and has the stage given to mimes the license that is allowed?
My poems too have often been danced before the people,
often they have even detained your eyes.
Surely, as in our homes the painted bodies of men of old
shine, the work of an artist's hand,
so somewhere there is a small panel that portrays
various embraces and the figures of love.
And as the son of Telamon sits, his anger confessed in his face,
and the barbarian mother has the crime in her eyes,
so dripping Venus dries her wet hair with her fingers,
and is seen now veiled by her mother's waters,
others sing of wars armed with learned weapons,
and part sings of your race, part of your deeds,
grudging Nature has confined me to a narrow space,
and given my talent slender strength,
and yet that fortunate author of your Aeneid
brought "arms and the man" to Tyrian beds,
nor is any part of the whole body read more
than the love joined by no lawful bond.
The same poet, in his youth, had earlier sported
in bucolic measures with the fires of Phyllis and tender Amaryllis,
I too long ago sinned in that kind of writing:
a fault not new suffers a new punishment;
and I had published poems while you, marking offenses,
I passed by so often, a knight unrebuked.
Therefore the writings which, as a youth, I thought would not harm me,
imprudent, have now harmed me as an old man.
Late has the vengeance for the old book overflowed,
and the punishment is far from the time of its deserving.
Yet, lest you think all my work is loose,
I have often given great sails to my ship.
I wrote six books of the Fasti, and as many,
and each roll has its end with its own month,
and this was lately written under your name, Caesar,
and my lot broke off the work dedicated to you;
and I have given a royal work written in tragic buskins,
and it has the words that the grave buskin should have,
and I have told, though the last hand was wanting to the work begun,
of bodies changed into new shapes.
And would that you might recall your mind a little from anger,
and at leisure bid a few things be read to you from here!
A few, in which, rising from the first origin of the world,
I have brought the work down to your times, Caesar!
You will see how much heart you yourself have given me,
and with what favor of mind I sing you and yours.
I have stripped no one with a biting poem,
nor does my verse hold the crimes of any,
candid, I have shrunk from witticisms steeped in gall:
no letter of mine is mixed with venomed jest.
Among so many thousands of our people, so many writings,
I shall be the one whom my Calliope has wounded.
I do not, then, foretell that any citizen rejoices
at my woes, but that many have grieved at them;
nor is it credible to me that any has insulted me as I lay,
if any thanks have been returned to my candor.
By these things, I pray, and by others may your divine power be bent,
O father, O care and safety of your country!
Not that I may return to Ausonia, unless perhaps one day,
when you are overcome by the long time of my punishment;
a safer exile and a little quieter I beg,
that my punishment may be equal to my fault.

title: Tristia
text:
1. If there shall be faults in my little books, as there will be,
hold them, reader, excused by their time.
I was an exile, and rest, not fame, was my aim,
that my mind might not be ever fixed on its own ills.
This is why even the digger, bound in his fetters, sings,
when he softens his heavy toil with an untrained measure.
He sings too, leaning forward on the muddy sand,
who drags the slow boat against the stream;
and he who brings the pliant oars together to his breast,
beats the water with his arms in time as the water is struck.
When the weary shepherd has leaned upon his staff or sat upon a rock,
he soothes his sheep with a reed-pipe's song.
Singing alike, alike drawing out her allotted task,
the slave-girl's labor is beguiled and cheated.
Sad Achilles too, they tell, when Lyrnesis was taken from him,
eased his cares with the Haemonian lyre.
When Orpheus drew the woods and hard rocks by singing,
he was mourning his twice-lost wife.
Me too the Muse comforts as I seek the appointed lands of Pontus.
She alone has stood firm, the companion of my flight;
she alone fears neither ambush, nor the Sintian soldier's sword,
nor sea, nor winds, nor barbarism.
She knows too, when I perished, what error deceived me,
and that there was fault in my deed, not crime,
just for this reason now kind, that she harmed me before,
when she was arraigned as defendant of a crime joined with me.
I would not indeed, since they were to harm me,
have laid my hand on the rites of the Muses,
but now what am I to do? The very power of those rites holds me,
and, mad, I love the poetry by which I was wounded.
So the lotus, new-tasted by the Dulichian palate,
was pleasant in the very flavor by which it harmed.
The lover for the most part feels his loss, yet clings to it,
and pursues the matter of his own fault.
I too am delighted by the little books, though they harmed me,
and I love the weapon that made my wounds.
Perhaps this pursuit may seem to be madness,
yet this madness has something of usefulness:
it ever forbids the mind to be fixed in the sight of its ills,
and makes it forgetful of present misfortune.
And as the Bacchant, wounded, feels not her own wound,
while she is rapt, screaming to the Idaean measures,
so when my breast grows warm, stirred by the green thyrsus,
that spirit is higher than human woe.
It feels not the exile, nor the shores of the Scythian sea,
it feels not that the gods are angry.
And as if I drank the cups of sleep-bringing Lethe,
so the sense of the adverse time is absent from me.
Rightly therefore I revere the goddesses who lighten my ills,
companions of an anxious flight from Helicon,
who deigned to follow my steps, part by sea, part by land,
whether by ship or on foot,
be these at least, I pray, kind to me! For the rest
of the gods' throng sides with great Caesar,
and heap me with as many woes as the shore has sands,
and as many fish, and fishes' spawn, as the sea has,
sooner shall you number the flowers in spring, the ears of grain in summer,
the apples in autumn, and the snows in the cold,
than the ills which, tossed over the whole world, I suffer,
while, wretched, I make for the leftward shores of the Euxine.
Yet, since I came, the fortune of my woes is no lighter:
hither too my fates have followed my ways.
Here too I recognize the threads of my birth,
threads made for me from a black fleece.
And, not to tell of snares and perils of my life,
true indeed, but graver than belief in the true,
how wretched it is to live among the Bessi and the Getae,
for one who was ever rushing in the people's mouth!
How wretched, to guard one's life by gate and wall,
and scarce to be safe by the strength of one's own place!
As a youth I shunned the harsh contests of soldiery,
nor handled arms save in sport;
now, an old man, I gird my side with sword, my left arm with shield,
and set the helmet upon my gray hairs.
For when the watchman from the lookout has given the signal of alarm,
straightway we don our arms with trembling hand.
The foe, holding bows and shafts steeped in venom,
savage, circles the walls on his panting horse,
and as a ravening wolf carries off and drags the sheep
that has not sheltered in the fold, through fields, through woods,
so, if the barbarian foe has found anyone in the plains
not yet received within the gates, he takes him:
he either follows captive, taking the chains cast on his neck,
or perishes by the venom-bearing weapon.
Here I, a new dweller, hide in an anxious abode.
Alas, the time of my fate is far too long!
And yet my Muse, a stranger amid such great ills,
holds out, that I may return to the numbers and the old rites,
but there is no one to whom I may recite my poems, nor who
may take in Latin words with his ears.
For myself—for what am I to do?—I write and read,
and my writing is safe in its own judgment.
Yet often I have said, "For whom does this care now labor?
Or will the Sauromatae and Getae read my writings?"
Often too tears were shed as I wrote,
and the letter was made wet by my weeping,
and my heart feels its old wounds as though new,
and the rain of sad water glides into my bosom,
when, by the turn of fate, I recall what I am and was,
and it comes to mind where chance has borne me, and whence.
Often, mad, my hand, angry at my pursuits and itself,
cast my poems into the fire to burn,
and so, since of many not many remain,
make it, whoever you are, that you read them with indulgence.
And you, Rome, forbidden to me, look kindly upon my song,
no better than my times, as the good.

title: Tristia
text:
2. Now savage Germany, like the whole world,
can have bent the knee, conquered, to the Caesars,
and the high Palatine may perhaps be veiled with garlands,
and incense sound in the fire and discolor the day,
and the white victim, struck on the neck by the drawn axe,
may beat the ground with its crimson blood,
and both the victorious Caesars prepare to render to the temples
the gifts of friends promised to the gods,
and the youths who grow up under Caesar's name,
that that house may rule the lands forever,
and Livia with the good brides give to the deserving gods
gifts for her son's safety, often to give them,
and the matrons together, and those who without stain
guard the chaste hearths with perpetual virginity;
let the pious commons and the senate with the pious commons rejoice,
of which I, a knight, was lately a small part.
Me, far expelled, the common joys escape,
and the news comes, from so far off, only small,
so all the people will be able to behold the triumphs,
and read the captured towns with the leaders' titles,
and see the kings bearing chains on their captive necks
go before the garlanded horses,
and discern the faces of some turned to suit the time,
of others terrible and unmindful of themselves,
of whom one part will ask the causes and the affairs and the names,
another will tell, though it knows too little.
"This man, who shines aloft in Sidonian purple,
was the leader of the war, that one next to the leader.
This one, who now fixes his pitiable eyes on the ground,
had not that face when he bore arms.
That one, fierce and still burning with hostile eyes,
was the urger of the battle and its counsel.
This treacherous one shut in our men by the snare of the ground,
who covers his squalid face with hanging hair.
By that one, who follows, they say, captured bodies were often
sacrificed to a god who refused them.
This lake, these mountains, these so many forts, so many rivers
were full of savage slaughter, full of gore.
Drusus once earned his title in these lands,
who was a good offspring, worthy of his parent.
Here, with broken horns, ill-covered by the green sedge,
the Rhine was discolored with his own blood.
Lo, Germany too is borne with disheveled hair,
and sits in mourning beneath the foot of the unconquered leader,
and, offering her spirited neck to the Roman axe,
bears chains in the hand with which she bore arms."
Above these, Caesar, you will ride in the victor's chariot,
in purple, fitly through the faces of your people,
and wherever you go, you will be clapped round by the hands of your own,
flowers thrown on every side covering the ways.
Your brows will be girt with Phoebean laurel, and "io,
io, great triumph!" the soldier will sing with mighty voice,
you yourself, amid the sound and applause and roar together,
will often see the four-horse team halt.
Thence you will seek the citadel and the shrines favorable to vows,
and the laurel of your vow will be given to deserving Jove.
These things, banished, I shall behold with the only mind I can:
that has the right of the place taken from me;
it ranges free over the boundless lands,
it reaches the sky by a swift way,
it leads my eyes into the midst of the city,
and does not let them be free of so great a good;
and the mind finds a place from which to view the ivory cars;
so at least for a brief time I shall be in my country.
Yet the happy people will catch the true spectacle,
and the throng will be glad, present with its leader.
But I must take in this fruit only by imagining,
and with ears far removed,
and, sent into a world far from Latium,
there will scarce be one to tell me, eager, of those things.
He too will tell of an already late and old triumph:
yet at whatever time I hear it, I shall be glad.
That day will come on which I lay aside my mourning,
and the public cause will be greater than my private one.

title: Tristia
text:
3. Greater and Lesser Bears, of whom one rules the Greek,
the other the Sidonian ships, both ever dry,
since, set on the highest pole, you behold all things,
and do not sink beneath the western waters,
and your circle, girding with its embrace the airy citadel,
stands clear of the untouched ground,
look, I pray, on those walls which once, they say,
Remus, son of Ilia, ill-fatedly leaped across,
and turn your shining faces to my mistress,
and tell me whether she is mindful of me or not.
Alas, why do I fear? I ask what is plain.
Why does my hope lie mixed with doubtful dread?
Believe what is, and what you wish, and cease to fear safe things,
and let your faith be sure of a sure fidelity,
and what the fires fixed in the pole cannot tell you,
tell yourself with a voice that will not lie,
that she is mindful of you, for whom you have the greatest care,
and that she keeps, as she can, your name with her.
She clings to your features as if you were present,
and, though removed far off, loves you, if only she lives.
And when your sick mind has lain down to its just grief,
does gentle sleep depart from your warned heart?
Then do cares come on, while bed and place
touch you, and do not let you be forgetful of me,
and does the fever come, and does the night seem endless,
and do the weary bones of your tossed body ache?
I do not doubt that these and other things befall,
and that your love gives signs of sad grief,
nor are you tormented less than when the Theban woman
saw bloody Hector dragged from the Thessalian car.
Yet what to pray for myself I doubt, nor can I say
what feeling of mind I would have you hold.
Are you sad? I am indignant that I am the cause of your grief;
are you not? Yet you would be worthy of a husband, if you had lost one.
But do you grieve your losses, most gentle wife,
and pass a sad time amid my ills,
weep for my misfortunes: there is a certain pleasure in weeping;
grief is filled and discharged by tears,
and would that you had to mourn not my life, but my death,
and that you were left alone by my death!
This breath would have gone out through you into my native air,
pious tears would have sprinkled my breast,
and on the last day, as my eyes gazed on the familiar sky,
your fingers would have closed them,
and my ash, laid in my ancestral tomb, would have rested,
and the earth I touched at birth would hold my body;
finally, as I lived, I should have died without reproach.
Now my life is shamed by its own punishment.
Wretched me, if you, when called the wife of an exile,
turn away your face and a blush comes to your cheeks!
Wretched me, if you think it shameful to be seen married to me!
