Wretched me, if now you are ashamed to be mine!
Where is that time when you used to boast of your husband,
and not to hide the name of your spouse?
Where is the time when—unless you do not wish those things recalled—
it pleased you, I remember, both to be called and to be mine?
And, as is worthy of a good woman, I pleased you with every gift:
your favoring love added much to the true.
Nor was there another man whom you would prefer—so great did I seem to you—
or whom you would rather have for your own.
Now too be not ashamed that you are married to me; your grief
should be here, your shame should be absent,
when rash Capaneus fell by a sudden stroke,
do you read that Evadne blushed for her husband?
Nor, because the king of the world checked fires with fires,
was Phaethon himself therefore to be denied.
Nor was Semele estranged from Cadmus, her father,
because she perished, ambitious, by her own prayers.
Nor let it bring a crimson blush to your soft face
that I am struck by the savage fires of Jove.
But rather rise to the care of guarding me,
and be to me the example of a good wife,
and fill the sad matter with your virtues:
glory goes by a steep and headlong path.
Who would know Hector, had Troy been happy?
The public way of virtue lies through ills.
Your art, Tiphys, lies idle, if there is no wave on the sea:
if men are well, your art, Phoebus, lies idle.
Virtue, which lies hidden and rests unknown in good fortune,
appears and is proved by ills.
My fortune gives you place for a title, and your devotion
has whereby to lift its head conspicuous.
Use the times, of whose gift it is now made,
and a wide field lies open for your praises.

title: Tristia
text:
4. O you who, though noble by the names of your ancestors,
surpass your stock by the nobility of your character,
in whose mind is the image of your father's candor,
yet so that that candor lacks not its own sinews,
in whose genius is the eloquence of your country's tongue,
than which there was none before in the Latin forum—
because I least wished it, you have been named by tokens
set in place of your name: forgive your own praises.
I have done no wrong; your known virtues betray you;
if you appear what you are, my fault is dissolved.
Nor do I think the service done you by my poem
can harm you, the prince being so just.
The father of his country himself—for what is more gracious than he?—
suffers to be read often in my poem,
nor can he forbid it, for Caesar is a public thing,
and of the common good my part too is a portion.
Jupiter grants his divine power to the genius of poets,
and lets himself be celebrated by any mouth,
your cause is safe by the example of two of the gods,
of whom one is seen, the other believed a god.
Though I ought not to have, yet I shall bear this charge:
it was not in your choice that my letter was sent.
Nor is it a new wrong of mine that I speak with you,
with whom, when unharmed, I often spoke.
That you may the less fear lest I, your friend, be a charge to you,
the author can bear the odium, if any there be,
for your father was ever cultivated by me from my earliest years—
do not, surely, dissemble this—
and he approved my genius—you can remember this—
even more than I, the judge, deserved;
and he spoke of my verses with the mouth
in which there was a part of his great nobility.
Therefore it is not now, because that house received me,
but earlier, that words were given to your father.
Nor were they given, believe me, yet: but in all my deeds,
if you take away the last, my life is to be defended.
This fault too, by which I perished, you will deny to be a crime,
if so great a part of the ill were known to you.
Either fear or error harmed me, error harmed me first.
Ah, let me not remember my fate;
nor, by handling them, let me break the wounds not yet closing:
scarce will rest itself profit them.
Therefore, as I justly pay the penalty, so all crime
and design were absent from my offense;
and the god feels this; for which neither was my light taken away,
nor does another possess the wealth not stripped from me.
Perhaps he will one day end this very flight—if only I live—
when his anger, with time, shall be milder.
Now I pray that he bid me depart hence to another place, if
my prayers lack not modest shame,
I wish a milder exile and a little nearer,
and a place farther from the savage foe;
and so great is the mercy in Augustus, that if anyone
should ask him this for me, perhaps he would grant it.
The cold shores of the Euxine Pontus hold me:
it was called Axenus, the inhospitable, by the ancients.
For neither are its waters tossed by moderate winds,
nor does the foreign ship approach its peaceful harbors.
Around are tribes that seek their plunder by blood;
nor is the land less feared than the faithless water.
Those whom you hear rejoice in human gore
lie almost under the axis of the same star,
nor is the place far from us where the Tauric altar
of the quivered goddess is sprinkled with dire slaughter.
This realm, before, as they tell, was not to be envied by the wicked
nor desired by the good, the realm of Thoas.
Here the Pelopean maid, in place of a substituted hind,
tended the rites of her goddess, such as they were.
Whither afterward—doubtful whether pious or wicked—Orestes,
driven by his own Furies, had himself come,
and his comrade, the Phocian, example of true love,
who were two in body, one in mind,
straightway they were bound and led to the grim altar,
which stood, bloody, before the twin doors.
Yet neither did his own death terrify the one, nor his the other;
each was sad for the other's death.
And now the priestess had stood with drawn blade,
and the barbarian fillet had girded the Greek hair,
when by the turn of speech she knew her brother, and to him
Iphigenia gave embraces in place of death,
and gladly, hating the cruel rites, she carried off the goddess's image
from those places to better ones.
This region, then, almost the last of the great world,
which men and gods flee, is near to me:
and near my land are the funereal rites,
if indeed a barbarian land is Naso's own.
O would that the winds by which Orestes was borne away
might bring back my sails too, the god appeased!

title: Tristia
text:
5. O you the first part among my beloved comrades,
the one altar found for my fortunes,
by whose words this dying soul revived,
as the watchful flame is wont with Pallas' oil poured on;
who feared not to open faithful harbors,
a refuge for the ship struck by the thunderbolt;
by whose wealth I should not have felt myself in want,
had Caesar snatched away my father's means.
While the impulse of this moment carries me, forgetful of the time,
alas, how nearly your name escaped me!
Yet you recognize yourself, and, touched by the desire of praise,
you would wish to be able to say openly, "It is I,"
surely I, if you allowed it, would give you the title,
and win for your fame a rare credence.
I fear to harm you, grateful one, by my poem, lest
the untimely honor of a name stand in your way,
what is allowed—and is safe—rejoice within your breast,
that I was mindful of you and that you were loyal,
and, as you do, strive at the oar to bring aid,
till a gentler breeze come with the god appeased;
and guard a life saveable by none, unless
he who sank it raise it from the Stygian water;
and show yourself constantly—which is rare—to every
service of unswerving friendship.
So may your fortune have perennial advances,
so may you not yourself need help, and may you aid your own,
so may your wife equal her husband in perennial goodness,
and may no quarrel fall upon your bed;
and may the partner of your blood ever love you with that
affection with which a pious brother loves Castor;
so may your son be a youth and like you, and may
anyone recognize him to be yours by his character;
so may your daughter make you a father-in-law by the marriage torch,
and give you, while still young, the name of grandfather.
6. The bond of our friendship, dearest one, you neither wish,
nor, should you wish it, can you dissemble,
for, while it was allowed, neither was another dearer to me than you,
nor was anyone in the whole city more joined to you than I,
and that love was so witnessed to the people, that it was
almost more known than you, and than I, were;
and the candor of your mind toward your dear friends—
those things are known to the very man you cherish.
You hid nothing so that I was not privy to it,
and gave many things to my breast to keep concealed:
and to whom I told whatever secret I had,
except that which ruined me, you were the only one.
Had you known that too, you would enjoy your comrade safe,
and by your counsel, my friend, I should be unharmed.
But my fates were dragging me, surely, to my punishment:
they close every road of useful good.
Whether I could have shunned this ill by caution,
or whether no reason avails to conquer fate,
yet you, O most joined to me by long intimacy,
almost the greatest part of my longing,
be mindful, and if your favor has made you any strength,
try those powers for me, I beg,
that the anger of the wronged power may be made milder,
and my punishment less by a changed place,
and so, if there is no crime in my breast,
and the beginning of my offense lies in error.
It is neither brief nor safe to tell by what chance
my eyes were made privy to the deadly ill;
and my mind shrinks back, as from its own wounds, from that time,
and at the reminder shame itself is renewed,
and whatever things can bring such shame,
it is fitting they be hidden, buried in blind night,
nothing, then, will I tell but that I sinned, but by that
sin no rewards were sought by me,
and that my crime should be called folly,
if you wish to give true names to the deed.
If these things are not so, seek another, farther from which I may be;
this place is a suburb to me here.

title: Tristia
text:
7. Go, hastily written letter, to greet Perilla,
faithful minister of my speech.
You will find her either sitting with her sweet mother,
or among her books and her own Muses.
Whatever she is doing, she will leave it when she knows you have come,
nor delay to ask why you come, or what I do.
You will say that I live, but so that I would not wish to live,
and that my ills are not lightened by so long a time,
and yet that I have returned to the Muses, though they harmed me,
and force fit words into alternating measures.
And do you say too, "Do you still cling to our common pursuits,
and sing learned poems, not in your father's manner?
For Nature, with the fates, gave you chaste morals
and rare gifts and genius.
This I first led to the Pegasid waters,
lest the vein of fertile water perish ill;
I first saw it in your tender maiden years,
and was, as a father to his daughter, your guide and companion.
Therefore, if the same fires remain in your breast,
the Lesbian poetess alone shall surpass your work.
But I fear lest my fortune now hold you back,
and after my misfortunes your heart be idle.
While it was allowed, I often read yours to me, mine to you;
often I was your judge, often your master:
either I gave my ears to verses just made,
or, where you flagged, I was the cause of your blushing.
Perhaps by my example, because the little books harmed me,
you too may have followed the fate of my punishment.
Lay aside, Perilla, your fear; only let no woman
nor man learn to love from your writings.
Therefore, most learned, remove the causes of your idleness,
and return to the good arts and your sacred rites.
That fair face will be marred by the long years,
and a senile wrinkle will be on your once youthful brow,
and ruinous old age, which comes with a step that makes no sound,
will lay its hand upon your beauty;
and when someone says, 'She was beautiful,' you will grieve,
and complain that your mirror lies.
Your means are modest, though you are most worthy of great ones:
but suppose them equal to boundless wealth,
surely Fortune gives whatever she pleases, and snatches it,
and he is suddenly Irus who was lately Croesus.
Not to tell each thing, we hold nothing immortal
save the good things of heart and mind.
Lo, I, who lack country and you and home,
and from whom is snatched whatever could be taken from me,
yet I myself company with and enjoy my own genius:
in this Caesar could have no right.
Let anyone end this life of mine with a savage sword,
yet, when I am dead, my fame will survive,
and while martial Rome, victorious, surveys from her hills
the whole conquered world, I shall be read.
You too, whom may a happier use of study await,
flee, as you can, the coming pyres while you may!"
8. Now I could wish to stand on the chariot of Triptolemus,
who sent the rude seed into the unknown soil;
now I would wish to rein the dragons of Medea,
which she had as she fled from your citadel, Corinth;
now I would long to take up wings to ply,
either yours, Perseus, or, Daedalus, yours:
that, the tender air yielding to my flights,
I might suddenly behold the sweet soil of my country,
and the face of my deserted home, and my mindful comrades,
and especially the dear face of my wife.
Fool, why do you vainly wish these things with childish vows,
which no day brings or will bring you?
If you must wish once, adore the divine power of Augustus,
and rightly pray to the god you have felt.
He can give you wings and winged cars:
let him grant return, and at once you are winged.
If I should pray for this—for I can ask no greater—
I fear my vows are too little modest.
Perhaps one day, when he has already sated his anger,
even then he must be asked with anxious mind.
What is less, meanwhile, I count for the likeness of an ample gift:
that he bid me go from here to any place.
Neither sky nor waters nor land nor air agree with me;
alas for me, a lasting languor holds my body!
Whether the contagions of a sick mind taint my limbs,
or the cause of my ill is in the region,
since I touched Pontus, sleeplessness vexes me, and scarce
does leanness cover my bones, nor does food please my mouth;
and the color that is in the leaves through autumn,
struck by the first cold, which the new winter has harmed,
that holds my limbs, nor am I relieved by any strength,
and the cause of querulous pain is never absent.
Nor am I better in mind than in body, but each part
is sick alike, and I bear a twofold loss.
There clings before my eyes, like a body to be seen,
the form of my fortune, standing to be read:
and when I behold the place, the manners of men, their dress, their tongue,
and it comes to mind who I am and who I was,
so great is my love of death that I complain of Caesar's anger
that he does not avenge his wrongs with the sword.
But since he has once used hatred in a civil way,
let my flight be lighter by a changed place.

title: Tristia
text:
9. Here too, then, are Greek cities—who would believe it?—
amid the names of inhuman barbarism;
hither too came settlers sent from Miletus,
and set up Greek homes among the Getae.
But the place has an older name, more ancient than the city's founding,
which is agreed to have come from the slaying of Absyrtus.
For in the ship which was made by the care of warlike Minerva,
the first to run through untried waters,
impious Medea, fleeing her deserted father,
is said to have plied her oars to these shallows.
When the watchman from a high mound saw it afar,
"A stranger comes," he said, "I know the sails of Colchis."
While the Minyae tremble, while the rope is loosed from the bank,
while the anchor follows the swift hands as it is dragged up,
the Colchian smote her breast, conscious of her deserts,
having dared, and yet to dare, many impious deeds with her hand;
and, though great daring remains in her mind,
pallor was on the face of the thunderstruck maiden.
Therefore, when she saw the approaching sails, "We are caught," she said,
"and my father must be delayed by some trick."
While she seeks what to do, while she turns her face to all things,
by chance she turned her bent eyes to her brother.
And when his presence was noted, "We have conquered," she said:
"this one shall by his death be the cause of my safety."
Straightway she pierces with rigid sword the innocent side
of the boy, unknowing and fearing no such thing,
and so tears him apart, and scatters the torn limbs
through the fields, to be found in many places,
and, lest her father not know, she sets on a high crag
the pale hands and the bloody head,
that the father, delayed by the new grief, and while he gathers
the slain limbs, might tarry on the sad journey.
Hence this place was called Tomis, because they say in it
the sister cut up the limbs of her brother.
10. If anyone there still remembers Naso, taken away,
and my name survives without me in the city,
let him know that, set beneath the stars that never touch the sea,
I live in the midst of barbarism.
The Sauromatae, a wild race, the Bessi and Getae surround me—
how unworthy names of my genius!
Yet while the air is warm, we are defended by the Hister between:
he, flowing, repels war with his waters,
but when grim winter has put forth her squalid face,
and the earth is made white with marble frost,
when Boreas and the snow forbid one to dwell beneath the Bear,
then these tribes plainly press, the pole trembling.
The snow lies, and, that the sun and rains may not dissolve it once cast,
Boreas hardens it and makes it lasting.
So when the first has not yet melted, another comes,
and in many places it is wont to remain two years;
and so great is the force of roused Aquilo, that he levels
high towers with the ground, and bears off the roofs he tears away.
With skins and stitched breeches they keep off the cruel cold,
and of the whole body only the face is exposed.
Often the hair tinkles, stirred, with the hanging ice,
and the white beard shines with the frost laid on it;
and wines stand bare, keeping the shape of the jar,
nor do they drink draughts of wine, but pieces given them.
Why should I tell how the streams, bound, freeze with cold,
and brittle waters are dug out of the pool?
The Hister itself, no narrower than the papyrus-bearing river,
which mingles with the vast sea through many mouths,
freezes its blue waters as the winds harden them,
and creeps into the sea with its waters roofed over;
and where ships had gone, men now go on foot, and the horse's hoof
beats the waves congealed with cold;
and over the new bridges, with the waters gliding beneath,
the Sarmatian oxen draw the barbarian wagons.
I shall scarce be believed, indeed, but, since there are no prizes
for falsehood, a witness ought to win sure credence:
I have seen the vast sea stand still with ice,
and a slippery crust pressed the motionless waters.
Nor is it enough to have seen; I have trodden the hard sea,
and the surface of the wave was under a foot not wet.
Had you once had such a strait, Leander,
your death would not be the crime of the narrow water.
Then neither can the curved dolphins lift themselves
into the air; the harsh winter checks them as they try;
and though Boreas roar with beaten wings,
there will be no wave in the besieged gulf;
and the ships, shut in by frost, will stand in the marble,
nor will the oar be able to cleave the rigid waters.
I have seen fish held fast, bound in the ice,
yet a part of them then too was alive.
Whether, then, the savage force of too great Boreas
freezes the waters of the sea, or those swollen by the river,
straightway, the Hister leveled by the dry Aquilos,
the barbarian foe rides in on his swift horse;
the foe, strong in horse and in the far-flying arrow,
lays waste the neighboring land far and wide.
Some flee, and, with none guarding the fields,
the unwatched wealth is plundered,
the small wealth of the country, cattle and creaking wagons,
and what riches the poor dweller has.
Part are driven captive, their arms bound behind their backs,
looking back in vain at their fields and homes:
part fall, wretchedly pierced with barbed arrows,
for there is a stained venom in the winged iron.
What they cannot carry off or lead away, they destroy,
and the enemy flame burns the innocent huts.
Even when there is peace, they tremble with the dread of war,
nor does anyone cleave the ground with pressed plowshare,
this place either sees or fears the foe it does not see;
the earth, abandoned, lies idle in rigid neglect.
Here no sweet grape lurks under the vine's shade,
nor do the boiling musts heap the deep vats.
The region denies fruit, nor would Acontius have here
whereon to write words for his mistress to read.
You would see bare fields, without leaf, without tree.
Alas, places not to be approached by a happy man!
So, when the vast world lies open so far and wide,
this is the land found out for my punishment!

title: Tristia
text:
11. If you are anyone, base man, who insults my misfortunes,
and, bloodthirsty, drives me on as a defendant without end,
you were born of crags and fed on the milk of a beast,
and I shall say that your breast holds flint.
What further step remains, to which your anger may reach?
Or what do you see lacking to my ills?
A barbarian land and the inhospitable shores of Pontus,
and the Maenalian Bear with her Boreas, behold me.
I have no commerce of tongue with the savage race:
all places are full of anxious fear.
And as the timid stag, caught by greedy bears,
or as the lamb hemmed in by mountain wolves trembles,
so I, fenced about on every side by warlike tribes,
am terrified, the foe almost pressing my side.
And though it were a small punishment that I lack my dear wife,
that I lack my country and my pledges of love:
though I bear no ill but Caesar's bare anger,
is Caesar's bare anger too little ill for me?
And yet there is someone who reopens my raw wounds,
and loosens his eloquent mouth against my character.
In an easy cause anyone may be eloquent,
and the least force avails to break what is shattered:
it is valor to overthrow citadels and standing walls;
any coward presses what is already fallen.
I am not what I was; why do you trample an empty shade?
Why do you assail my ashes and tomb with stones?
Hector was Hector when he warred; but the same
was not Hector when bound to the Haemonian horses.
Remember that I too, whom you once knew, am not:
of that man these phantoms survive.
Why, fierce one, do you assail phantoms with words, lover?
Spare, I beg, to trouble my shade!
Suppose all my crimes true, that there be in them nothing
which you would think rather error than wickedness,
lo, I, a fugitive, pay the penalty—sate your breast
with punishments grievous by exile and by the place of exile.
My fortune might seem worthy of an executioner's tears:
yet to one judge alone it is too little drowned.
You are crueler than grim Busiris, crueler than him
who terrified the false bull with the slow fire,
and who is said to have given the bull to the Sicilian tyrant,
and to have commended his arts with these words:
"In this gift, king, there is use, but more in the image,
nor is the form of my work alone to be approved.
Do you see this side of the bull, openable on the right?
Into this must be cast whoever you would destroy.
Straightway burn him, shut in, with slow coals:
he will bellow, and that voice will be a true bull's.
For these inventions, that you may pay gift with gift,
give, I beg, rewards worthy of my genius."
He had spoken, but Phalaris, "Wondrous inventor of punishment,
yourself, present, baptize your work," he said.
Nor was there delay: cruelly burned by the fires he had shown,
he gave forth from his groaning mouth twin sounds.
What have I to do with Sicilians, here among Scythia and the Getae?
To you, whoever you are, my complaint returns,
and that you may slake your thirst with my blood,
and bear as much joy as you wish in your greedy heart,
I have suffered so many ills fleeing by land, so many by sea,
that I think you too could grieve at hearing them,
believe me, if Ulysses be compared with me,
Neptune's anger was less than Jove's has been.
Therefore, whoever you are, do not reopen my crimes,
and take your hard hands from my grievous wound;
and, that forgetfulness may thin the fame of my fault,
let my deeds draw a scar;
and, mindful of the human lot, which lifts the same men
and presses them down, dread yourself the uncertain turns.
And since—what I thought could never be—
you have the greatest care for my affairs,
there is no cause for you to fear. My fortune is most wretched,
Caesar's anger draws every ill with it.
And that this may be the plainer, lest I be thought to feign it,
I myself could wish that you might try my punishments.

title: Tristia
text:
12. Now the Zephyrs lessen the cold, and, the year being ended,
the Maeotic winter has seemed longer than of old,
and he who bore Helle ill, set upon him,
makes the times of night equal to the day,
now boys and merry girls gather the violet,
which springs up wild, sown by no one;
and the meadows grow green with the flower of varied colors,
and the chattering bird, untaught, sings in the spring;
and that she may lay aside the crime of an evil mother, the swallow
makes her cradle and small dwelling beneath the beams;
and the herb that lurked, buried in the Cerealian furrows,
comes forth and spreads its soft tip from the ground;
and where there is a vine, the bud is moved from the shoot:
for far from the Getic shore the vine is absent;
and where there is a tree, the branch swells on the tree:
for far from the Getic borders the tree is absent.
There is leisure now in your land, and, with the games joined in order,
the chattering wars of the wordy forum give way. There is sport
now of the horse, now men play with light arms,
now the ball, now the hoop is rolled in a swift circle;
now, when the youth is anointed with the gliding oil,
they bathe their wearied limbs in the Virgin water.
The stage flourishes, and favor burns for differing pursuits,
and the three theaters resound for the three forums.
O four times, O how often—it cannot be numbered—blest
is he to whom it is allowed to enjoy the city not forbidden!
But by me the snow is felt, melted by the spring sun,
and the waters which are no longer dug hard from the pool.
Nor does the sea congeal with ice, nor, as before, along the Hister
does the Sauromatian herdsman drive his creaking wagons.
Yet some keels will begin to swim hither,
and a guest ship will be on the shore of Pontus.
Eagerly I shall run to the sailor, and, the greeting given,
ask why he comes, and who he is, and from what places.
He, indeed, it would be strange if he had not, safe,
plowed only the near waters from a neighboring region.
Rare is the sailor who crosses so great a sea from Italy,
rare he who comes to these harborless shores,
yet whether he know how to speak in the Greek or Latin
tongue—surely the latter's will be the more welcome;
and it is possible that someone, from the mouth of the strait and the long Propontis,
has set sail hither with a steady South Wind—
whoever he is, he can report a rumor with mindful voice,
and become a part and a step of report.
He, I pray, may be able to tell of Caesar's triumphs heard,
and of vows paid to Latian Jove,
and that you, rebellious Germany, at last
have set your sad head beneath the feet of the great leader.
He who tells me these things, which I shall grieve not to have seen,
will straightway be a guest in my house.
Alas for me, is Naso's house now in the Scythian world?
And does my punishment give me its place for a home?
Grant, you gods, that Caesar wish this to be not my inner shrine and home,
but the lodging-place of my punishment.
13. Lo, superfluous—for what use was it to be born?—
my birthday comes to its own season,
hard one, why did you come to the wretched years of an exile?
You ought to have set an end to them.
If you had any care for me, or any shame within you,
you would not have followed me beyond my country,
and in the place where I, an infant, was first ill-known to you,
there you would have tried to be my last,
and at my leaving, what my comrades did themselves,
you too would have said, sad, "Farewell," in the city.
What have you to do with Pontus? Did Caesar's anger send you too
to the farthest ground of the icy world?
You expect, no doubt, the honor of your accustomed rite,
that a white robe hang from my shoulders,
that the smoking altar be girt with flowering garlands,
and the grain of incense crackle in the solemn fire,
and that I give cakes that fitly mark my natal time,
and frame good prayers with favoring mouth.
I am not so placed, nor are these the times for me,
that I can be glad at your coming.
A funeral altar, girt with the death-cypress, suits me,
and the flame prepared on the built-up pyre.
Nor does it please me to give incense that entreats the gods for nothing,
nor in such great ills do good words come to me.
Yet if there is anything to be sought by me on this day,
I pray that you come no more to these places,
while Pontus, almost the last part of the world,
called Euxine by a false name, holds me.

title: Tristia
text:
14. Cultivator and holy priest of learned men,
what do you, ever friend to my genius?
Do you, as you used once to celebrate me unharmed,
now too take heed that I may not seem wholly absent?
Do you take up my poems, only the Art excepted,
which harmed its own maker?
Nay, do so, I beg, student of new poets,
and, as you can, keep my body in the city.
Flight is decreed me, not decreed to my little books,
which did not deserve their master's punishment.
Often a fugitive father is exiled to foreign shores,
yet his children may dwell in the city.
After the example of Pallas, born of no mother, my poems
were created of me; this is my stock and offspring.
This I commend to you, which, the more bereft of its parent,
the greater burden it will be to you, its guardian.
I have three children who have followed my contagion:
make the rest of the throng your care openly.
There are also the changed forms, fifteen rolls,
poems snatched from their master's funeral.
That work could have had a surer name from the finishing hand,
had I not perished first myself:
now, uncorrected, it has come into the people's mouths,
if anything of mine is in the people's mouth at all.
This too, whatever it is, add to my little books,
which comes to you sent from another world.
Whoever shall read it, if anyone shall read it, let him weigh first
at what time and in what place it was composed.
He will be fair to writings of which he has learned that
their time was exile, and their place barbarism;
and amid so many adversities he will marvel that any poem
I had the heart to draw out with a sorrowful hand.
My ills have broken my genius, whose spring even before
was unfruitful and whose vein was scant.
But whatever it was, with none to exercise it, it has shrunk,
and, dried up, perished by long neglect.
Here is no store of books to invite and feed me;
in place of books, bows and arms resound,
none in this land, if I recite poems, is present
whose understanding ears I might use;
there is no place where I may withdraw. The guard of the wall
and the closed gate keep off the hostile Getae.
Often I seek some word, a name, a place,
nor is there anyone from whom I might be more sure.
Often, attempting to say something—shameful to confess!—
words fail me, and I have unlearned how to speak.
The Thracian and Scythian tongue resounds almost on every side,
and I seem able to write in Getic measures.
Believe me, I fear lest Pontic words be mixed in
with the Latin, and that you read them in my writings.
Such as it is, then, deem the little book worthy of pardon,
and excuse it by the condition of my lot.
1. If anything in my little books should be flawed—as it will be—
forgive it, reader, in view of the time that made it.
I was an exile, and it was rest I sought, not fame,
that my mind might not be fixed forever on its woes.
This is why even the chained ditch-digger sings,
easing his heavy toil with an untaught measure.
He sings too who, bent over the muddy shoal, hauls
his slow barge upstream against the current;
and he who draws the supple oars in time to his chest,
beating his arms as the beaten water beats them back.
When the weary shepherd has leaned on his staff or settled on a rock,
he soothes his flock with a song from his reed-pipe.
The maid, singing as she spins her allotted task,
beguiles and cheats her labour by the same.
They say that grieving Achilles, when the Lyrnessian girl was taken,
lightened his cares upon the Haemonian lyre.
When Orpheus drew the woods and the hard rocks by his singing,
he was mourning his bride twice lost.
Me too the Muse relieves as I make for the place I was bidden, Pontus.
She alone stood firm, companion of my flight;
she alone fears no ambush, no Sintian soldier's sword,
no sea, no winds, no barbarian land.
She knows, too, what error undid me when I fell,
that there was fault in my deed, but no crime.
Just now indeed she is fair to me, since before she did me harm,
when she was charged as defendant in the crime joined with mine.
I would not, since they were bound to bring me harm,
have laid my hand upon the rites of the Muses;
but now what am I to do? The very power of those rites holds me,
and, mad, I love the song that wounded me by song.
So the lotus, once tasted by the Dulichian palate,
was sweet in flavour, even by that which harmed.
The lover generally feels his own losses, yet clings to them,
and pursues the very stuff of his own undoing.
I too take delight in my little books, though they have harmed me,
and I love the weapon that dealt my wounds.
Perhaps this devotion may seem to be madness,
yet this madness has something of use in it:
it forbids the mind to be always intent on its sorrows,
and makes it forget the present mischance.
And as the Bacchant, wounded, feels not her own hurt,
while she raves, shrieking to the Idaean strains,
so when my breast is stirred and warmed by the green thyrsus,
that spirit rises higher than human ill.
It feels not exile, nor the shores of the Scythian sea,
it feels not that the gods are wrathful.
And as if I drank cups of sleep-bearing Lethe,
so the sense of my adverse hour is taken from me.
With right, then, I revere the goddesses who lighten my woes,
companions from Helicon of my anxious flight,
who deigned to follow my steps, partly by sea, partly by land,
whether by ship or on foot.
Be these, I pray, at least kind to me! For of the gods
the rest take sides with great Caesar,
and heap on me as many troubles as the shore has sands,
as the strait has fish, as a fish has eggs.
You will sooner number the flowers in spring, the ears of corn in summer,
the fruits through autumn, the snows in the cold,
than the ills which, tossed across the whole world, I endure,
while in misery I seek the leftward shores of the Euxine.
Yet, since I came, the fortune of my woes is no lighter:
here too my fate has followed in my tracks.
Here too I recognize the threads of my birth-star,
threads spun for me from a black fleece.
And, not to tell of ambushes and perils to my life—
true indeed, but heavier than truth will credit—
how wretched it is to live among the Bessi and the Getae
for one who once rushed always on the people's lips!
How wretched to guard one's life by gate and wall,
and scarcely to be safe even by the strength of one's own place!
In youth I shunned the hard contests of war,
nor handled weapons except in play;
now, an old man, I gird my side with sword, my left arm with shield,
and set the helmet upon my grey head.
For when the watchman from his tower gives the signal of attack,
at once with trembling hand we put on our arms.
The savage foe, with bows and arrows steeped in poison,
circles the walls on his panting horse,
and as the ravening wolf bears off and drags
through fields and woods the sheep that found no fold,
so, if the barbarian enemy finds any in the open
not yet received within the gates, he takes him:
either he is led away captive, his neck receiving the cast chains,
or he perishes by a weapon that holds venom.
Here I lie hidden, a new dweller in an anxious home.
Alas, too long the span of my fate!
And yet the Muse, a guest amid such great ills,
endures to return to verse and her old rites,
but there is no one to whom I may recite my songs, none
to take in Latin words with his ears.
For myself—what else am I to do?—I both write and read,
and my page is safe before its own judge.
Yet often I have said: "For whom does this labour toil now?
Or will the Sauromatae and Getae read my writings?"
Often, too, as I wrote, the tears poured forth,
and the letter was made wet by my weeping,
and my heart feels its old wounds as though they were new,
and the rain of mournful water glides into my breast,
when, by the change reversed, I recall what I am and what I was,
and there comes upon me where fate has borne me and from where.
Often my mad hand, in anger at my studies and itself,
has cast my songs into the fire to burn,
and so, since of many few survive,
read these, whoever you are, with indulgence.
And you, Rome, forbidden to me, look kindly—
no better than my times—upon my song.

title: Tristia
text:
2. Now savage Germany, like all the world, may—
conquered—have sunk with bended knee before the Caesars,
and the high Palatine perhaps is veiled with garlands,
and incense crackles in the fire and dims the day,
and the gleaming victim, its neck struck by the lifted axe,
beats the ground with its crimson blood,
and both Caesars prepare to render to the temples of the kindly gods
the gifts their friends had vowed,
and the young men who grow up under the Caesarean name,
that that house may rule the earth forever,
and Livia, with her good daughters-in-law, for her son's safe return
gives gifts to the gods who earned them, and will often give,
and with her the mothers, and those who, blameless,
guard the chaste hearths in perpetual virginity;
the pious commons, and with the pious commons the Senate, rejoice,
the Senate of which I lately was a small part, a knight.
Far off, expelled, the common joys pass me by,
and only a little of the news, from so far, reaches me.
So all the people will be able to watch the triumphs,
and read on the leaders' placards the captured towns,
and see the kings, chains on their captive necks,
walking before the garlanded horses,
and will mark the faces of some changed by the moment,
of others terrible and forgetful of themselves.
Some of the crowd will ask the causes, the deeds, the names;
some will tell, though they know but little.
"This man, who shines aloft in Sidonian purple,
was leader of the war; that next one, second to the leader.
This one, who now fixes his pitiful gaze on the ground,
had not that look when he bore his arms.
That fierce one, his eyes still burning with hatred,
was the urger of battle and its counsellor.
This treacherous one shut in our men by the snare of the terrain,
he who hides his squalid face with hanging hair.
By that one who follows, they say, captured bodies were often
sacrificed, though he refused, to his god.
This lake, these mountains, all these forts, all these rivers
were full of savage slaughter, full of blood.
Drusus once earned in these lands the name
that, a noble son, was worthy of his parent.
That one with broken horns, ill-covered by green sedge,
was the Rhine, discoloured by his own blood.
Lo, Germany too is led with streaming hair,
and sits in grief beneath the foot of the unconquered chief,
and, offering her proud neck to the Roman axe,
she bears the chains on the hand with which she bore her arms."
Above these, Caesar, in your victor's car you will be borne,
robed in purple, duly through your people's gaze,
and wherever you go you will be acclaimed by your people's hands,
and the way will be strewn everywhere with scattered flowers.
Your brow will be wreathed with Phoebus' laurel, and the soldier
will chant "Io triumph!" with mighty voice,
and amid the sound and applause and roar together you will often
see the four-yoked horses halt at the singing.
Thence you will seek the citadel and the shrines that favour vows,
and the due laurel will be paid to Jupiter for your vows.
This, far removed, I shall behold with such mind as I can:
that mind has the right to a place taken from me.
It ranges free across the boundless lands,
it comes by a swift road into heaven,
it leads my eyes into the heart of the city,
and lets them not be deprived of so great a good;
and the spirit finds a place from which to watch the ivory car;
so at least I shall be in my homeland for a brief while.
Yet the happy people will catch the true spectacle,
and the throng present with its prince will be glad.
But for me, only by imagining, and with ears far removed,
this fruit must be gathered here,
and, sent far from Latium into a world apart,
scarcely will there be one to tell me, eager, of these things.
He too will report a triumph already late and old:
yet whenever I hear of it, I shall be glad.
That day will come when I shall lay aside my mourning,
and the public cause will outweigh the private.

title: Tristia
text:
3. Greater Bear and Lesser, of whom one guides the Greek,
the other the Sidonian ships, both never setting,
since, placed at the summit of the sky, you see all things,
and do not sink beneath the western waters,
and your circle, girdling with its embrace the airy citadel,
stands clear above the untouched earth,
look, I pray, upon those walls which once, they say,
Remus, son of Ilia, leapt across—and ill it went for him—
and turn your bright faces toward my lady,
and tell me whether she is mindful of me or not.
Ah, why do I fear? I ask what is plain.
Why does my hope lie mixed with wavering dread?
Believe what is so and what you wish, and cease to fear the safe,
and let your sure faith be sure of certain faith,
and what the flames fixed in the pole cannot tell you,
tell to yourself in a voice that will not lie:
that she is mindful of you, for whom your greatest care is,
and keeps, as she can, your name with her.
She clings to your face as though you were present,
and, though removed far off, she loves you, if only she lives.
Tell me—when the sick mind has sunk into its just grief,
does gentle sleep depart from the warned heart?
Then do cares come on, while the bed and the place and you
touch her and let her not forget me,
and the fever comes, and the night seems endless,
and the weary bones of her tossing body ache?
I doubt not indeed that these and other things befall,
and that your love gives signs of mournful grief,
and that you are tortured no less than when Theban Andromache
saw bloodied Hector dragged from the Thessalian car.
Yet I doubt what I myself should pray, nor can I say
what feeling of mind I would have you keep.
Are you sad? I am vexed that I am the cause of your grief;
are you not? Then you would deserve to lose your husband.
But mourn your own losses, gentlest of wives,
and spend a grim time amid my ills,
weep for my misfortunes: there is a certain pleasure in weeping;
grief is filled out and worked off by tears.
And would that you had to mourn not my life but my death,
and had been left alone by my death!
This breath would have passed, through you, into my native air,
pious tears would have wet my breast,
and on the last day my eyes, gazing at the familiar sky,
would have been closed by your fingers,
and my ashes, set in the ancestral tomb, would have rested,
and the soil that touched my birth would hold my body;
in short, as I had lived, so I would have died without crime.
Now my life is shameful by its own punishment.
Wretched me, if you, when called the wife of an exile,
turn away your face and the blush comes to your cheeks!
Wretched me, if you think it shameful to be seen wed to me!
Wretched me, if now you are ashamed to be mine!
Where is that time when you used to boast
of your husband, nor hide the name of your man?
Where is the time when—unless you will not have it recalled—
it pleased you, I remember, both to be called and to be mine?
And as is fitting for a virtuous wife, I pleased you with every gift:
favouring love added much to the truth.
Nor was there a man you would prefer to me—so great I seemed to you—
nor whom you would rather have as your own.
Now too be not ashamed that you are wed to me; your grief
should not be absent from this, but your shame should.
When rash Capaneus fell by a sudden stroke,
do you read that Evadne blushed for her husband?
Nor, because the king of the world quenched fires with his fires,
was Phaëthon himself to be disowned.
Nor was Semele made a stranger to her father Cadmus,
because she perished, ambitious, by her own prayers.
Nor, because I have been struck by Jove's fierce fires,
let a crimson blush come upon your soft cheek.
But rise rather to the care of guarding me,
and be to me the example of a good wife,
and fill with grim matter your virtues:
glory walks its steep path by a sheer way.
Who would know of Hector, had Troy been happy?
The public road of virtue is made through misfortunes.
Your art, Tiphys, lies idle, if there is no wave on the sea;
if men are healthy, Phoebus, your art lies idle.
The virtue that lies hidden and stays unknown in good times
shows itself and is proved by misfortunes.
My fortune gives your renown its place, and gives your devotion
the means to lift its head conspicuous.
Use the times whose gift it now is made,
and a wide field lies open for your praises.

title: Tristia
text:
4. O you who, noble as you are by the names of your ancestors,
surpass your line by the nobility of your character,
in whose mind is the image of your father's candour,
yet so that that candour lacks not its own sinews,
in whose talent is your country's eloquence of tongue,
than which there was none greater before in the Latin forum—
since, much against my will, I have named you by your marks
in place of your name: forgive your own praises.
I have done no wrong; your own merits, once known, betray you;
if you appear what you are, my fault is dissolved.
Nor do I think that the homage paid you in my song
can harm you under a prince so just.
The Father of his Country himself—for what is more civil than he?—
endures to be read often in my song,
nor can he forbid it, for Caesar is the commonwealth's,
and of the common good a part is mine as well.
Jupiter lends his godhead to the genius of poets,
and suffers himself to be celebrated by any mouth.
Your case is safe by the example of two gods,
of whom one is seen, the other believed, divine.
Though I ought not to have, yet I shall bear this charge:
the choice of writing to you was not yours.
Nor is it a new offence of mine that I speak with you,
with whom, when safe, I often spoke.
And that you may fear the less lest a friend be a charge to you,
the blame, if there is any, the author of it can bear,
for your father—do not, surely, conceal this—
was cherished by me always from my earliest years,
and he approved my talent (you can remember this)
even more than I, in my own judgment, deserved;
and he spoke about my verses with that mouth
in which was a part of his great nobility.
So it is not now to you, because that house received me,
but first to your father, that words were given.
Yet they were not given—believe me—but in all my acts,
if you take away the last, my life must be defended.
This fault too, by which I perished, you will deny to be a crime,
if so great a part of my ill be known to you.
Either fear or error harmed me, but error came first.
Ah! let me not remember my fate;
nor by handling them let me reopen wounds not yet closed:
even rest will scarcely profit them.
So, as I justly pay the penalty, so every crime
and design was absent from my offence;
and the god knows it; for which neither was my light taken,
nor does another possess my wealth, stripped from me.
Perhaps this very flight, if only I live, he will one day end,
when his anger has grown gentler with time.
Now I pray that he bid me depart hence to another place, if
my prayers are not without modest shame,
a milder exile, a little nearer, I ask,
and a place farther from the savage foe;
and so great is the clemency in Augustus, that if someone
should ask this for me of him, perhaps he would grant it.
The cold shores of the Euxine Pontus confine me:
"the Inhospitable" it was called by the ancients of old.
For neither are its waters tossed by moderate winds,
nor does the visiting ship reach calm harbours.
Around are tribes that seek plunder by bloodshed;
and the land is feared no less than the treacherous water.
Those whom you hear rejoice in human blood
lie almost beneath the axis of the same star,
nor is the place far from us where the dread Tauric
altar of the quivered goddess is sprinkled with slaughter.
This realm, they tell, was once not coveted by the wicked,
nor to be desired by the good—the realm of Thoas.
Here the Pelopian maid, in place of a substituted deer,
tended such rites as she could for her goddess.
After Orestes had come here, driven by his own Furies—
whether pious or guilty is doubtful—
and his companion, the Phocian, example of true love,
who, two in body, were one in mind,
at once they are led, bound, to the grim altar,
which stood bloody before the twin doors.
Yet his own death did not affright this one, nor his own that one:
each was grieving for the other's death.
And now the priestess had taken her stand with drawn blade,
and had bound the barbarian fillet on their Greek hair,
when, by an exchange of speech, she knew her brother, and to him
Iphigenia, instead of death, gave an embrace,
and, glad, transferred the image of the goddess who loathed cruel rites
from those parts to better ones.
This region, then, almost the last of the great world,
which men and gods flee, lies near to me;
and near my land are funeral rites,
if indeed the barbarian land is Naso's own.
O would that the winds by which Orestes was carried away
might bear my sails too, when the god is appeased!

title: Tristia
text:
5. O first part among the comrades I have loved,
my fortunes' one altar found,
by whose words this dying soul revived,
as the wakeful flame revives when oil is poured upon it;
you who did not fear to open faithful harbours
and refuge to a vessel struck by the thunderbolt;
by whose wealth I should not have felt myself in want,
had Caesar snatched away my ancestral riches.
While the impulse of this moment carries me, forgetful of the time,
your name has nearly—alas!—slipped from me!
Yet you recognize it, and, touched by desire of praise,
"That is I," you would wish to be able to say openly.
Surely I, if you allowed it, would gladly render you the title,
and win for it the rare credit of fame.
I fear to harm you, though grateful, by my song, and lest
the untimely honour of being named should stand in your way;
what is permitted—and is safe—rejoice within your breast,
that I am mindful of you, and that you were loyal,
and, as you do, strive with the oars to bring me aid,
until a softer breeze comes from a calmer god;
and guard a head that none can save, unless
he who plunged it lift it from the Stygian water;
and show yourself constant—which is rare—to every
duty of unswerving friendship.
So may your fortune have unending advancement,
so may you yourself need no help and aid your own,
so may your wife match her husband in lasting goodness,
and no quarrel fall upon your marriage-bed;
and may your brother by blood ever love you with that
affection by which the loyal brother loves Castor;
so may your son be a youth like you, and may anyone
recognize by his ways that he is yours;
so may your daughter make you a father-in-law by the wedding torch,
and give you, while still young, the name of grandfather not late.
6. In time the bull grows patient of the ploughman's plough,
and offers his neck to be pressed by the curved yoke;
in time the spirited horse obeys the supple reins,
and takes the hard bits in his gentle mouth;
in time the rage of Punic lions is curbed,
nor does the fierceness that was before remain in their hearts;
and the Indian beast, which obeys the orders of its keeper,
in time, conquered, submits to servitude.
Time makes the grape swell with its lengthening clusters,
till the seeds within scarcely hold the wine they have;
time brings forth the seed into whitening ears,
and takes care that the fruits be not of a bitter taste.
This wears down the share of the plough that renews the soil,
this wears hard flint, this wears adamant;
this, too, little by little softens fierce angers,
this lessens grief and lightens the mournful heart.
All things, therefore, slipped away with silent foot, can age diminish,
except my cares.
Since I lost my homeland, twice has the threshing-floor been trodden of its grain,
twice has the grape, pressed by the bare foot, burst apart.
Yet no patience has been won in so long a span,
and my mind keeps the sense of its ill as if fresh;
indeed old oxen too often flee the yoke,
and the horse, broken to the bridle, often fights it.
And my present trouble is grimmer than the former:
for though it is equal to itself, it has grown and swelled with delay.
Nor were my ills so well known to me as they are;
now they weigh the more, the more they are known.
It is no small thing, too, to bring fresh strength,
and not to be already worn out by time's hardships.
The new wrestler is stronger on the tawny sand
than he whose arms are weary, slowed by delay.
The whole gladiator is better in his gleaming armour
than he whose weapons are red, dyed with his own blood.
The newly made ship bears the headlong storms well:
the old one is loosed apart by however small a rain.
We too bore more patiently what we bear,
before our ills were multiplied by the long day.
Believe me, I am failing, and, as far as I divine
from my own body, but little time is added to my woes.
For neither is my strength what it was, nor the colour I used to have:
scarcely have I a thin skin to cover my bones.
But my mind is sicker than my sick body, and stands
without end in the contemplation of its own ill.
The look of the city is far away, far my comrades, my care,
and she than whom none is dearer to me, my wife, is far.
The Scythian rabble is here, the trousered throng of the Getae:
thus both what I see and what I do not see move me.
Yet there is one hope that may console me in these things—
that these ills will not be long, by reason of my death.

title: Tristia
text:
7. Twice has the sun come to me after the cold of icy winter,
and twice run its course, touching the Fish.
In so long a time why has your right hand
done no kindly service in verses, however few?
Why has your loyalty ceased, when they wrote
with whom I had but little intimacy?
Why, as often as I loosed the bindings of some sheet,
did I hope that it bore your name?
May the gods grant that your letter often was written
by your right hand, though none of the many reached me.
What I pray, it is plain, is so. Sooner would I believe Medusa's face,
the Gorgon's, was girt with snaky hair,
that there are dogs beneath the maiden's womb, that the Chimaera is,
which parts a lioness from a savage serpent by flames,
and four-footed creatures joined with a human breast,
and the triple man and the triple dog,
and the Sphinx and the Harpies and the serpent-footed Giants,
and hundred-handed Gyas and the half-bull man.
All these I would sooner believe than that you, dearest,
have changed and laid aside your care for me.
Countless mountains lie between me and you, and roads
and rivers and plains and not a few straits.
By a thousand causes it may be that a letter, often
sent by you, comes rarely into my hands;
yet overcome the thousand causes by writing often,
that I may not always have to excuse you, friend, to myself.
8. Now my temples mimic the swan's plumage,
and white old age stains my dark hair,
now come the frail years and the more sluggish time of life,
and now it is hard for me to bear myself, scarcely firm.
Now was the time when, my labours laid aside,
I ought to live, troubled by no fear,
and to enjoy the leisure that always pleased my mind,
and gently to be at my studies,
and to honour my small house and the old household gods,
and the ancestral fields that now lack their master,
and, in my lady's arms and among dear comrades,
to grow old, secure, in my homeland.
So once had this age of mine hoped to be passed:
so I deserved to lay down these years.
The gods thought not so, who, driving me by land and sea,
have cast me forth into Sarmatian lands.
The battered ships are led into the hollow docks,
lest they break up rashly in mid-water.
Lest he fall and dishonour the many palms he has won,
the horse, grown weak, crops the grass in the meadows.
When the soldier is no longer fit enough in his years of service,
he lays down at the old household gods the arms he bore.
So then, as slow old age lessens my strength,
for me too it was now time to be given my wooden sword.
It was time not to draw a foreign air,
nor to ease a parched thirst at the Getic spring,
but to withdraw into the empty gardens I once had,
to enjoy again the sight of men and the city.
So once, my mind not divining the future,
I longed to be able to live in peace as an old man.
The Fates fought against it; they, who gave me my early times
soft, weigh down the later ones.
And now, ten lustres ended without a stain,
I am pressed in the worse part of my life,
and not far from the goals which I seemed almost to grasp,
a heavy crash has befallen my course.
So, mad, have I forced him to rage against me,
than whom the boundless world holds nothing gentler?
And was clemency itself overcome by my offences,
and yet was life not denied to my error?
A life to be passed far from my homeland, beneath the Northern axis,
where the left-hand land of the Euxine sea lies.
If Delphi and Dodona itself had told me this,
both places would have seemed empty of truth.
Nothing is so strong, though adamant bind it,
as to stand firmer than the swift fire of Jove;
nothing is so lofty and stretches beyond perils,
that it is not below and subject to a god.
For though part of my ills was contracted by my fault,
yet the godhead's anger gave more of ruin.
But be you too warned by my misfortunes,
to earn the favour of a man who equals the gods.

title: Tristia
text:
9. If you permit and allow it, I shall keep silent the name and the deed,
and your acts shall be given to the waters of Lethe,
and my clemency shall be won over by late tears,
only make it plain that you have repented of yourself;
only make it plain that you condemn yourself and wish to erase
the time of your life, if you could, those Tisiphonean years.
But if not, and your breast burns with hatred of me,
then unhappy grief will put on enforced arms.
Though I am sent, as I am, into the farthest world,
my anger will stretch out its hands from here.
Caesar—if you do not know it—left me all my rights,
and my only penalty is to lack my homeland.
And my homeland, if only he be safe, I hope for from him:
often the oak, scorched by Jove's bolt, grows green again.
In short, if there is no means of vengeance for me,
the Muses will give their powers and their weapons.
Though I dwell far removed on the Scythian shores,
and the nearest constellations are dry to my eyes,
my proclamation shall go through boundless nations,
and what I complain of shall be known as far as the world stretches.
Whatever I say shall go from the east to the west,
and the East shall be witness to my Western voice.
I shall be heard across the land, across the deep waves,
and the cry of my groan shall be loud,
nor shall your own age alone know you guilty:
you shall be a reproach to lasting posterity.
Already I am borne into the fray, and have not yet taken up my horns,
nor would I wish there to be any cause for taking them up.
The Circus is still idle; already the grim bull
scatters the sand and now beats the ground with hostile hoof.
This too is more than I wished. Sing, Muse, the retreat,
while he is allowed to hide his name.
10. I who was once the playful poet of tender loves,
that you may know me, hear, posterity, who I was.
Sulmo is my homeland, rich in cool streams,
ninety miles distant from the city.
Here I was born, and—that you may know the time—
when both consuls fell by a like fate.
If it is anything, I am an heir to the rank from of old, through my forebears,
no knight made only by fortune's gift.
Nor was I the firstborn son; I was begotten after a brother
who had come into the world three times four months before.
The same Morning Star was present at both our births:
one day was celebrated with two cakes.
This is the first of the five festivals of armed Minerva,
the first that is wont to be made bloody by combat.
At once, while young, we are educated, and by our father's care
we go to men distinguished in the arts of the city.
My brother from his green age aimed at eloquence,
born for the strong arms of the wordy forum,
but to me even as a boy the heavenly rites were pleasing,
and the Muse was secretly drawing me to her work.
Often my father said, "Why do you attempt a useless study?
Homer himself left no riches."
I was moved by his words, and, leaving all Helicon,
I tried to write prose free of metre.
Of its own accord a song came into fitting measures,
and what I tried to write was verse.
Meanwhile, as the years glided by with silent step,
the freer toga was taken by my brother and me,
and the purple with the broad stripe was put on our shoulders,
and the study that was before remained ours.
And now my brother had doubled his ten years of life,
when he died, and I began to lack a part of myself.
We took also the first honours of tender age,
and I was once one of the board of three men.
The Senate-house remained: the breadth of my stripe was narrowed;
that burden was greater than my strength.
Neither was my body able, nor my mind fit for the toil,
and I was one shy of anxious ambition,
and the Aonian sisters urged me to seek safe
leisure, ever loved by my judgment.
The poets of that time I cherished and cultivated,
and as many bards as were present, I thought gods were present.
Often Macer, older in age, read me his birds,
and the snake that harms, the herb that helps.
Often Propertius was wont to recite his fires,
by the right of the fellowship by which he was joined to me.
Ponticus, famed in epic, Bassus too, famed in iambics,
were sweet members of my circle.
And tuneful Horace held our ears,
while he struck cultured songs on the Ausonian lyre.
Virgil I only saw; nor did grudging fate give Tibullus
time for my friendship.
He was your successor, Gallus, and Propertius his;
fourth from these in the order of time was I myself.
And as I cherished the elder poets, so the younger cherished me,
and my Thalia became known not slowly.
When first I read my youthful songs to the people,
my beard had been cut but once or twice.
She had stirred my genius, sung through the whole city,
whom I called by no true name, Corinna.
Much indeed I wrote, but what I judged faulty
I myself gave to the fires to mend.
Then too, when I went into exile, I burned some that would have pleased,
in anger at my study and my songs.
Soft was my heart, not impregnable to Cupid's darts,
and such that the lightest cause could move it.
Yet though I was such, and was kindled by the smallest fire,
no scandal was raised under my name.
While still almost a boy I was given a wife neither worthy nor useful,
who was my bride for a brief time.
Her there succeeded a wife who, though without fault,
was not destined to be firm in my bed.
The last, who stayed with me into my later years,
endured to be the wife of an exiled husband.
My daughter, twice fruitful in her first youth,
but not by one husband, made me a grandfather.
And now my father had completed his fated span,
and added nine more lustres to his nine.
I wept no otherwise than he would have wept for me, had I been taken.
Next I bore my mother to the grave.
Happy both, and buried in good time,
who perished before the day of my punishment!
Happy I too, that not while they lived
am I wretched, and that they grieved for nothing concerning me!
Yet if of the dead anything but the name remains,
and the slender shade escapes the built-up pyres,
if, parents' shades, the report of me has reached you,
and my charges are heard in the Stygian court,
know, I pray—for it is not right for me to deceive you—
that the cause of my ordered flight was error, not crime.
This is enough for the shades: to you I return, eager
hearts, who seek the deeds of my life.
Already, my better years driven away, grey hairs
had come to me, and mingled with my old locks,
and ten times since my birth the victorious knight,
crowned with the Pisan olive, had borne off the prizes,
when the anger of the wounded prince bade me seek
the Tomitae, set on the left of the Euxine sea.
The cause of my ruin, too well known to all,
must not be attested by my own witness.
Why tell of comrades' wickedness and harmful slaves?
I bore many things no lighter than the exile itself.
My mind scorned to yield to its ills, and proved
itself unconquered, using its own strength;
and, forgetful of myself and of a life spent in leisure,
I took up with unaccustomed hand the arms of the time;
and I bore as many mishaps by land and sea as there are stars
between the hidden and the visible pole.
Touched at last, driven by long wanderings,
was the shore where the Sarmatian joins the quivered Getae.
Here, though I am ringed round by neighbouring arms,
I ease my grim fate by such song as I can.
And though there is no one to whose ears it may be brought,
yet thus I use up and beguile the day.
So that I live and hold out against my hardships,
nor are the wearinesses of the anxious light upon me—
thanks, Muse, to you: for you give solace,
you come as rest from care, you come as medicine.
You are my leader and companion, you lead me away from the Hister,
and give me a place in the midst of Helicon;
you have given me, while alive—a rare thing—a lofty
name, which fame is wont to give from the funeral rites,
nor has Envy, who disparages things present,
bitten any work of mine with grudging tooth.
For though our age has borne great poets,
fame has not been grudging to my genius,
and though I set many above myself, I am called no less than they,
and through the whole world I am most widely read.
If, then, the prophecies of poets have any truth,
even if I die at once, I shall not, earth, be yours.
Whether by favour or by my song I have won this fame,
rightly to you, kind reader, I give thanks.

title: Tristia
text:
1. This little book too, devoted reader, from the Getic
shore add to the four I sent before.
This too will be such as the poet's fortune is:
you will find nothing sweet in the whole song.
As my state is mournful, so is the song mournful,
the writing suiting its matter.
Whole and happy, I played at happy, youthful things;
yet now it grieves me to have composed them.
Since I fell, I proclaim my sudden mischance,
and am myself the author of my own theme.
And as the Caystrian bird, lying on the bank,
is said to wail its own death with failing voice,
so I, cast far out upon the Sarmatian shores,
see to it that my funeral does not pass in silence.
If anyone seeks delights and wanton songs,
I warn him: there is no reason for him to read these.
Fitter for him will be Gallus and Propertius of the winning mouth,
fitter Tibullus, of charming genius.
Would that I were not numbered among them!
Ah me, why did my Muse ever jest?
But I have paid the penalty, and on the borders of the Scythian Hister
that player of the quivered Love is absent.
What is left, I have turned my mind to public songs,
and have bidden men be mindful of my name.
Yet if any one of you should ask of me so much—
whence I sing what is to be mourned—I have borne much to mourn.
These I compose not by genius, not by art:
the matter is ingenious by its own ills.
And how small a part of my fortune is in the song?
Happy he who suffers what he can number!
As many as the shrubs of the wood, as the yellow sands of the Tiber,
as the soft grasses the field of Mars has,
so many ills have I endured, whose cure and rest
is in nothing but study and the Muses' tarrying.
"What measure, Naso, of your tearful song?" you ask.
The same that the measure of this fortune will be.
What I complain of, it supplies me from a full spring,
nor are these words mine, but those of my fate.
But if you should give me back my homeland with my dear wife,
my face would be cheerful, and I would be what I was before.
If the anger of unconquered Caesar were milder to me,
I would now give you songs full of gladness.
Yet my writing shall not play again, as it once played;
let it have run riot once in my jest.
What he himself may approve, I shall sing, if only the penalty be eased in part,
and I escape the barbarism and the harsh Getae.
Meanwhile, what should my little books do but mourn?
That flute suits my funerals.
"But you could," you say, "bear your ills better by silence,
and, saying nothing, hide your misfortunes."
You demand that no groans follow torments,
and forbid me to weep when struck by a grievous wound?
Phalaris himself allowed the man in the Perillean bronze
to utter bellowings and to complain with a bull's mouth.
Since Achilles was not offended by Priam's tears,
do you, harder than the foe, check my weeping?
When Latona's offspring made Niobe childless,
yet she did not bid her keep her cheeks dry too.
It is something to lighten a fated ill by words.
This made one a Procne, another a Halcyon.
This was why, in his cold cave, the son of Poeas
wearied the Lemnian rocks with his voice.
Grief shut in chokes and seethes within,
and is forced to multiply its strength.
Grant pardon rather, or take away my books entirely,
if what profits me harms you, reader.
But it cannot harm, nor have my writings ever been
fatal to any but their author.
"But they are bad." I confess it. Who forces you to take up the bad?
Or who forbids you, deceived, to lay down what you took up?
I myself do not amend them, but that they be read as written;
they are no more barbarous than their place.
Nor should Rome compare me with her poets:
among the Sauromatae I was a genius.
In short, no glory is sought by me, nor the fame
that is wont to set spurs to talent.
I do not wish my mind to waste away with constant cares,
which yet break in and go even where they are forbidden.
Why I write, I have told; why I send to you, you ask—
because I long to be with you in any way at all.

title: Tristia
text:
2. When a new letter comes from Pontus, do you grow pale,
and is it opened by your anxious hand?
Lay aside your fear, I am well; and the body which before
was impatient of toils and weak in me,
holds out, and, harassed, has hardened by the very use.
Or is it that I have no leisure to be ill?
Yet my mind lies sick, and has taken no strength with time,
and the passion of soul that was before remains.
And the wounds I thought would close with delay and their own span
ache no otherwise than if just made.
True, time's long age helps small ills;
to great ills harms accrue with time.
For nearly ten whole years the son of Poeas nursed
the pestilent wound dealt by the swollen serpent.
Telephus would have perished, consumed by endless wasting,
had not the hand that harmed brought help.
And I—if I have committed no crime—pray that he who made
my wounds may be willing to ease what he has made,
and, content at last with a part of my grief,
take a little water from a full sea;
that though he draw off much, much of bitterness will remain,
and a part of my penalty will be as great as the whole.
As many shells as the shores have, as many flowers as the pleasant rose-beds,
as many seeds as the sleep-bringing poppy holds,
as many beasts as the wood feeds, as many fish as swim the wave,
as many as the birds that beat the soft air with wings,
by so many adversities am I pressed: which if I should try to grasp,
I should try to tell the number of the Icarian waters.
And, to say nothing of the road's mishaps, the bitter perils of the sea,
to say nothing of the hands drawn against my life,
a barbarous land and the last of the great world
holds me, and a place ringed by a savage foe.
From here I would be moved—for my fault is not bloody—
were there in you, as there ought to be, care for me.
That god, on whom the Roman power is well based,
has often been mild, as victor, toward his foe.
Why do you hesitate and fear what is safe? Approach and ask:
nothing in the vast world is gentler than Caesar.
Wretched me! What shall I do, if my nearest abandon me?
Do you too withdraw your neck from the broken yoke?
Where shall I be borne? Whence seek solace for my weary affairs?
No anchor now holds my vessel.
See to it! I myself, though hated, will flee to the holy altar:
the altar drives away no hands.
Lo, absent, I address absent powers in supplication,
if it is right for a man to be able to speak with Jove:
arbiter of empire, by whose safety it is certain that all
the gods have care for the Ausonian race,
O glory, O image of the homeland that flourishes through you,
O man no smaller than the very world you rule—
so may you dwell on earth, and the heavens long for you,
so may you go late to the stars promised to you—
spare me, I pray, and take away the least part
of your thunderbolt! Penalty enough will remain.
Your anger indeed has been moderate, and you gave me life,
and I lack neither a citizen's right nor my name,
nor was my fortune granted to others, nor am I named
an exile in the words of your edict.
And all these things I feared, because I saw I deserved them;
but your anger is gentler than my offence.
You bade me, banished, look upon the fields of Pontus,
and cleave the Scythian strait with a fugitive ship;
ordered, I came to the ugly shores of the Euxine
sea—this land lies beneath the cold axis—
nor does the sky, never without frost, torment me so,
and the clod always scorched by hoary cold,
and that the barbarian tongue knows no Latin speech,
and Greek is conquered by the Getic sound,
as that, ringed about, I am pressed on all sides by neighbouring war,
and a thin wall scarcely makes me safe from the foe.
Peace there sometimes is, but trust in peace never:
so this place now suffers, now dreads, arms.
From here let me be moved, and let Zanclean Charybdis
devour me and send me to the Styx with her waters,
or let me be burned, patient, in the flames of swift Aetna,
or be cast into the deep straits of the Leucadian god.
What I seek is a punishment: for I do not refuse to be wretched,
but I pray that I may be wretched more safely.

title: Tristia
text:
3. This is the day on which the poets are wont to celebrate you,
Bacchus, if only the seasons deceive me not,
and bind their festal brows with fragrant garlands,
and chant your praises over your wine.
Among them, I remember, while my fate allowed me,
I was often a part not unwelcome to you,
whom now the Sarmatian shore, set beneath the stars
of the Cynosurian Bear, joined to the raw Getae, holds,
and who once led a soft life, free of toils,
in study and in the Muses' choir,
now far from my homeland am ringed by Getic arms,
having suffered much before by sea and much by land.
Whether chance gave me this or the anger of the gods,
or a cloudy Fate was mine at birth,
yet you ought to have upheld with your godhead
one of the worshippers of your sacred ivy.
Or does whatever the sisters, mistresses of fate, have chanted
cease to be at the disposal of a god?
You yourself were borne to the airy heights by your merits,
to which the way was made by no slight toil.
Nor did you dwell in your homeland, but came as far as snowy
Strymon and the Mars-worshipping Getan,
and Persia, and the Ganges roaming with broad stream,
and whatever waters the dark Indian drinks.
Surely the Parcae, spinning the threads of fate, chanted
this law to you, twice born, twice.
Me too, if it is right to go by the examples of the gods,
an iron lot of life and a hard one presses.
I fell no more lightly than he whom, speaking great things,
Jupiter drove from Thebes with his own fire.
Yet, when you heard that the bard was struck by the thunderbolt,
you could grieve at your mother's warning,
and, looking around upon the poets at your rites,
you could say, "Some worshipper of mine is missing."
Bring aid, good Liber: so may the vine weigh down
another elm, and the grape be full with enclosed wine,
so may the young company of Satyrs be with you
amid the Bacchae, and may you not be silent amid the frenzied din,
so may the bones of axe-bearing Lycurgus lie ill at ease,
nor may the impious shade of Pentheus be free of punishment,
so may the bright crown of your wife flash forever
in the sky and outshine the neighbouring stars.
Come here and ease our misfortunes, most beautiful one,
mindful that I am one of your number.
There is commerce among the gods: try to bend
Caesar's godhead, Bacchus, by your godhead.
You too, partners of my study, pious throng, poets,
ask each this same thing, your wine taken up.
And let one of you, when Naso's name is spoken,
set down his cup mingled with his tears,
and, reminded of me, when he has looked round upon all,
let him say, "Where is Naso, lately a part of our choir?"
And so, if I have earned your favour by my candour,
and no writing of mine has been hurt by my judgment,
if, while I worthily revere the writings of the men of old,
I deem the later ones not less than they—
so, then, may you make song by Apollo's favour:
keep, what is permitted, my name among you.
4. From the Euxine shore I, Naso's letter, have come,
made weary by the sea and weary by the road,
who, weeping, said to me, "You, to whom it is allowed, look upon Rome.
Alas, how much better is your lot than my lot!"
Weeping too he wrote me, nor was the gem with which I was sealed
brought first to his mouth, but to his wet cheeks.
If anyone seeks to know the cause of his sadness,
he asks that the sun be shown him,
he sees neither leaf in the woods, nor the soft grasses
in the open meadow, nor water in the full river;
he will wonder why Priam grieves, when Hector was carried off,
or why Philoctetes groans, struck by the serpent.
Would that the gods had granted such a state in him,
that the cause of his sadness need not be mourned!
Yet he bears, as he must, his bitter misfortunes patiently,
nor, like an untamed horse, refuses the bridle.
Nor does he hope the godhead's anger will be perpetual against him,
conscious that in his fault there is no crime.
Often he tells how great is the god's clemency, among whose
examples he is wont to number himself as well:
for that he keeps his ancestral wealth, that the name of citizen,
in short, that he lives, he holds to be the god's gift.
Yet you (O, if you believe me at all, dearer to him
than all) he has always in his whole heart;
and he calls you his Menoetiades, you who accompanied Orestes,
he calls you his Aegides and his Euryalus.
Nor does he long more for his homeland and for what,
most of all, his homeland feels to be absent from him,
than for your face and your eyes, O sweeter to him
than the honey that the Attic bee lays in its combs.
Often, too, grieving, he recalls that time,
which he mourns was not forestalled by death;
and when others fled the contagion of his sudden ruin,
nor would approach the threshold of the stricken house,
he remembers that you, with a few, stayed faithful to him,
if anyone calls three or two a few.
Though stunned, he yet felt all, nor that you
grieved at his adversities less than he himself.
He is wont to recall your words and your face and your groans,
and that your breast was wet as you wept;
how you stood by him, with what aid you consoled your friend,
when you yourself at the same time needed consoling.
For these things he affirms he will be mindful and pious,
whether he see the day or be covered by the earth,
swearing as he is wont by his own head and yours,
which I know is no cheaper to him than his own.
Full thanks will be returned for deeds so many and so great,
nor will he let your oxen plough the shore.
Only do this: guard the exile constantly. What he,
who knows you well, does not ask, I myself ask.

title: Tristia
text:
5. The yearly birthday of my lady demands its accustomed honour:
go, my hands, to the pious rites.
